**Bernard Jean Étienne Arnault**[[a]](#cite_note-2) (born 5 March 1949) is a French businessman. He is the chairman and [chief executive officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_executive_officer "Chief executive officer") (CEO) of [LVMH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LVMH "LVMH"), the world's largest [luxury goods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luxury_goods "Luxury goods") company.[[2]](#cite_note-3)[[3]](#cite_note-4) Arnault is [one of the richest individuals in the world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_World's_Billionaires "The World's Billionaires"); as of December 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bernard_Arnault&action=edit), he has an estimated net worth of [US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_dollar "United States dollar")190.4 billion according to *[Forbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbes "Forbes")* and [US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_dollar "United States dollar")203 billion according to the *[Bloomberg Billionaires Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomberg_Billionaires_Index "Bloomberg Billionaires Index")*.[[4]](#cite_note-5)[[5]](#cite_note-6)

Born in [Roubaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roubaix "Roubaix"), Arnault was raised in a devoutly Catholic household. He studied [civil engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_engineering "Civil engineering") and mathematics at [École Polytechnique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/École_Polytechnique "École Polytechnique"), graduating in 1971.[[6]](#cite_note-Team-7) He began his career in his father's company, Ferret-Savinel, shifting its focus to real estate, which laid the groundwork for his future career in the luxury goods market.

Arnault's entry into the luxury sector was marked by his strategic acquisition in 1984 of the financially-struggling textile and retail conglomerate Boussac Saint-Frères, which included the prestigious fashion house [Christian Dior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dior "Dior"). His aggressive business strategies earned him the nickname "The Terminator", as he revitalized Dior and sold off other assets for profit. In 1987, he played a key role in the creation of LVMH (an abbreviation for Louis Vuitton Moët Hennessy), a global luxury goods company, by merging [Louis Vuitton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Vuitton "Louis Vuitton") with Moët Hennessy. Through a series of strategic acquisitions and investments, Arnault built LVMH into a leading company in the luxury industry, overseeing significant growth and expansion into various sectors, including fashion, jewelry, watches, and wine.

Arnault's influence extends beyond LVMH, with investments in web companies and philanthropic endeavors, particularly in the arts. Following the 2019 [Notre-Dame fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notre-Dame_fire "Notre-Dame fire") in Paris, he donated €200 million to the rebuilding efforts.[[7]](#cite_note-8) He has also been involved in notable real estate and yacht ventures. His leadership has led to LVMH becoming the largest company by market capitalization in the [eurozone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurozone "Eurozone"). Despite controversies, including his attempt to become a Belgian citizen, Arnault's business acumen has solidified his status as a key figure in the global luxury market.

## Early life and education

Bernard Jean Étienne Arnault was born on 5 March 1949 in [Roubaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roubaix "Roubaix").[[8]](#cite_note-LVMH_bio-9)[[9]](#cite_note-France24-10) His mother, pianist Marie-Josèphe Savinel, daughter of Étienne Savinel, had a "fascination for [Dior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dior "Dior")".[[9]](#cite_note-France24-10) His father, manufacturer Jean Léon Arnault, a graduate of [École Centrale Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/École_Centrale_Paris "École Centrale Paris"), owned the civil engineering company Ferret-Savinel.[[9]](#cite_note-France24-10) Raised in a "strict Catholic-Auvergne" style by his devoutly Catholic grandmother, Arnault took classical piano lessons as a child and was educated at Catholic schools,[[10]](#cite_note-11)[[11]](#cite_note-12) the Lycée Maxence Van Der Meersch in Roubaix and the [Lycée Faidherbe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lycée_Faidherbe "Lycée Faidherbe") in [Lille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lille "Lille"),[[12]](#cite_note-La_Voix_du_Nord-13)[[13]](#cite_note-NYT_2007-14) which takes [boarders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boarding_school "Boarding school") and [prepares them for the *grandes écoles*.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classe_préparatoire_aux_grandes_écoles "Classe préparatoire aux grandes écoles")[[14]](#cite_note-15)

In 1971, he finished his studies in civil engineering and mathematics at French university [École Polytechnique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/École_polytechnique "École polytechnique") in 1971[[6]](#cite_note-Team-7)[[15]](#cite_note-16)

## Career

In 1971, soon after his graduation, Arnault began work for his father's company.[[9]](#cite_note-France24-10) Three years later, after he convinced his father to shift the focus of the company to real estate, Ferret-Savinel sold the industrial construction division and was renamed Ferinel. Following the acquisition of a textile company and relocation of its headquarters, the company renamed the real estate branch to the George V Group. The real estate assets were later sold to Compagnie Générale des Eaux (CGE), eventually becoming [Nexity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nexity "Nexity").[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

### 1971–1987: Professional start

Arnault began his career in 1971, at [Ferret-Savinel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nexity "Nexity"), and was its president from 1978 to 1984.[[9]](#cite_note-France24-10)[[13]](#cite_note-NYT_2007-14) In 1984, Arnault, then a young real estate developer, heard that the French government was set to choose someone to take over the Boussac Saint-Frères empire, a textile and retail conglomerate that owned [Christian Dior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dior "Dior").[[16]](#cite_note-:0-17)

With the help of Antoine Bernheim, a [senior partner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senior_partner "Senior partner") of [Lazard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lazard "Lazard") Frères, Arnault acquired the [Financière Agache](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financière_Agache "Financière Agache"), a [luxury goods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luxury_goods "Luxury goods") company.[[17]](#cite_note-:4-18) He became the CEO of Financière Agache and subsequently won the bidding war for Boussac Saint-Frères, buying the group for a ceremonial one franc and effectively taking control of Boussac Saint-Frères. After Arnault bought Boussac, he laid off 9,000 workers in two years, after which he acquired the nickname "The Terminator".[[16]](#cite_note-:0-17) He sold nearly all of the company's assets, keeping only the Christian Dior brand and Le Bon Marché department store.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] By 1987, the company was profitable again and booked earnings of $112 million on a revenue stream of $1.9 billion.[[17]](#cite_note-:4-18)

### 1987–1989: Co-founding and acquisition of LVMH

See also: [LVMH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LVMH "LVMH")

He worked with Alain Chevalier, CEO of Moët Hennessy, and [Henry Racamier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Racamier "Henry Racamier"), president of [Louis Vuitton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Vuitton "Louis Vuitton"), to form LVMH in 1987.[[18]](#cite_note-19)

In July 1988, Arnault provided $1.6 billion to form a holding company with [Guinness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guinness "Guinness") which held 24% of LVMH's shares. In response to rumors that the Louis Vuitton group was buying LVMH's stock to form a "blocking minority", Arnault spent $600 million to buy 13.5% more of LVMH, making him LVMH's largest shareholder. LVMH had been created on the premise that the conglomerate would be too large for a single hostile raider.[[16]](#cite_note-:0-17) However, the premise failed to take into account internal takeover attempts. The fault became too large to ignore when Arnault had a differing strategic vision from Racamier, Louis Vuitton's president.[[19]](#cite_note-:2-20)

In January 1989, he spent another $500 million to gain control of a total of 43.5% of LVMH's shares and 35% of its voting rights, thus reaching the "blocking minority" that he needed to stop the dismantlement of the LVMH group.[[19]](#cite_note-:2-20) He then turned on Racamier, stripped him of his power, and ousted him from the board of directors.[[16]](#cite_note-:0-17) On 13 January 1989, he was unanimously elected chairman of the executive management board.[[19]](#cite_note-:2-20)

### 1989–2001: LVMH's initial expansion and growth

After assuming leadership, Arnault led the company through an ambitious development plan, transforming it into one of the largest luxury groups in the world, alongside Swiss luxury giant [Richemont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richemont "Richemont") and French-based [Kering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kering "Kering").[[20]](#cite_note-:3-21) In eleven years, annual sales and profit rose by a factor of 5, and the [market value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_capitalization "Market capitalization") of LVMH increased by a factor of 15. In July 1988, Arnault acquired [Céline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Céline_(brand) "Céline (brand)").[[17]](#cite_note-:4-18) That same year, he sponsored French fashion designer [Christian Lacroix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Lacroix "Christian Lacroix") to advertise the company's luxury clothing line.[[19]](#cite_note-:2-20) LVMH acquired [Berluti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berluti "Berluti") and [Kenzo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenzo_(brand) "Kenzo (brand)") in 1993, the same year Arnault bought out the French economic newspaper *[La Tribune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Tribune "La Tribune")*.[[21]](#cite_note-22) La Tribune never achieved the desired success, despite his 150 million euro[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] investment, and he sold it in November 2007 to buy a different French economic newspaper, *[Les Échos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_Échos_(France) "Les Échos (France)")*, for €240 million.[[22]](#cite_note-23)[[23]](#cite_note-24)

In 1994, LVMH acquired the perfume firm [Guerlain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guerlain "Guerlain").[[24]](#cite_note-25) In 1996, Arnault bought out [Loewe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loewe,_S.A. "Loewe, S.A."),[[25]](#cite_note-26) followed by [Marc Jacobs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Jacobs "Marc Jacobs") and [Sephora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sephora "Sephora") in 1997.[[26]](#cite_note-27) Five more brands were also integrated into the group: [Thomas Pink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Pink "Thomas Pink") in 1999, [Emilio Pucci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emilio_Pucci "Emilio Pucci") in 2000, and [Fendi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fendi "Fendi"), [DKNY](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DKNY "DKNY"), and [La Samaritaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Samaritaine "La Samaritaine") in 2001.

In the 1990s, Arnault decided to develop a center in New York to manage LVMH's presence in the United States. He chose Christian de Portzamparreke to supervise this project.[[27]](#cite_note-28) The result was the [LVMH Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LVMH_Tower "LVMH Tower") that opened in December 1999.[[28]](#cite_note-29) That same year, Arnault turned his eyes to [Gucci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gucci "Gucci"), an Italian leather goods company, which was run by [Tom Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Ford "Tom Ford") and [Domenico De Sole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_De_Sole "Domenico De Sole"). He discreetly amassed a 5 percent stake in the company before being detected.[[16]](#cite_note-:0-17) Gucci responded hostilely and called it a "creeping takeover". Arnault then upped his stake to 34.4 percent while insisting he wanted to be a supportive and unassertive stakeholder. De Sole proposed that in return for board representation, Arnault would stop increasing his stake in Gucci. However, Arnault rejected this proposal. De Sole discovered a loophole that allowed him to issue shares with only board approval, and for every share LVMH bought, he created more for his employees, thus diluting Arnault's stake. The fight dragged on until a settlement in September 2001. After the legal ruling, LVMH sold its shares and realized a profit of $700 million.[[16]](#cite_note-:0-17)

In 1998, with businessman [Albert Frère](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Frère "Albert Frère"), Arnault purchased [Chteau Cheval Blanc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chteau_Cheval_Blanc "Chteau Cheval Blanc") in a personal capacity. LVMH acquired Arnault's share in 2009[[29]](#cite_note-30) to add to the group's other wine property [Chteau d'Yquem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chteau_d'Yquem "Chteau d'Yquem").

From 1998 to 2001, Arnault invested in a variety of web companies such as [Boo.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boo.com "Boo.com"), Libertysurf, and [Zebank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zebank "Zebank") through his holding Europatweb. Groupe Arnault also invested in [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix") in 1999.[[30]](#cite_note-31)

### Since 2001: Increasing success and profitability

In 2007, Blue Capital announced that Arnault owned jointly with the California property firm [Colony Capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colony_Capital "Colony Capital") 10.69% of France's largest supermarket retailer and the world's second-largest food distributor [Carrefour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrefour "Carrefour").[[31]](#cite_note-32)

In 2008, he entered the yacht business and bought [Princess Yachts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princess_Yachts "Princess Yachts") for 253 million euros.[[32]](#cite_note-33) He subsequently took control of [Royal van Lent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feadship "Feadship") shipyard for an almost identical amount.[[33]](#cite_note-34)

From 2010 until 2013, Arnault was a member of the Board of Advisors of the Malaysian [1MDB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1MDB "1MDB") fund.[[34]](#cite_note-35)[[35]](#cite_note-36)[[36]](#cite_note-37)[[37]](#cite_note-38)

On 7 March 2011, Arnault announced the acquisition of 50.4% of family-owned shares of the Italian jeweler [Bulgari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgari "Bulgari"), to make a tender offer for the rest, which was publicly owned.[[38]](#cite_note-39) The transaction was worth $5.2 billion.[[39]](#cite_note-40) In 2011, Arnault invested $641 million in establishing LCapitalAsia.[[40]](#cite_note-MW_March_72-41) On 7 March 2013, *National Business Daily* reported that mid-priced clothing brand QDA would open stores with the assistance of Arnault's private equity firm LCapitalAsia and Chinese apparel company Xin Hee Co., Ltd. in Beijing.[[40]](#cite_note-MW_March_72-41) In February 2014, Arnault entered into a joint venture with the Italian fashion brand Marco De Vincenzo, taking a minority 45% stake in the firm.[[41]](#cite_note-42)[[42]](#cite_note-LVMH_Takes_Stake_in_Marco_de_Vincenzo-43) In 2016, LVMH sold DKNY to [G-III Apparel Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G-III_Apparel_Group "G-III Apparel Group").[[43]](#cite_note-44) In April 2017, Arnault announced the acquisition of Christian Dior haute couture, leather, both men's and women's ready-to-wear, and footwear lines, which integrated the entire Christian Dior brand within LVMH.[[44]](#cite_note-bof-christian-dior-45)

By January 2018, Arnault had led the company to record sales of €42.6 billion in 2017, 13% over the previous year, as all divisions turned in strong performances. That same year, the net profit increased by 29%.[[45]](#cite_note-46) In November 2019, Arnault planned to acquire [Tiffany & Co.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiffany_&_Co. "Tiffany & Co.") for approximately US$16.2 billion. The deal was expected to close by June 2020.[[46]](#cite_note-47) LVMH then stated in September 2020 that the takeover would not proceed and that the deal was "invalid" because Tiffany mishandled the business during the COVID-19 pandemic.[[47]](#cite_note-marketscreener-48) Subsequently, Tiffany filed suit against LVMH, asking the court to compel the purchase or to assess damages against the defendant; LVMH planned to counter-sue, alleging that mismanagement had invalidated the purchase agreement.[[48]](#cite_note-49) In mid-September 2020, a reliable source told  [*Forbes*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbes_(magazine) "Forbes (magazine)") that the reason for Arnault's decision to cancel the Tiffany purchase was purely financial: Tiffany was paying millions in dividends to shareholders despite a financial loss of US$32 million during the pandemic. Upon examination of financial records, Arnault discovered that some US$70 million had already been paid out by Tiffany, with an additional US$70 million scheduled to be paid in November 2020.[[49]](#cite_note-50) LVMH filed a counterclaim against the court action commenced by Tiffany; a statement issued by LVMH blamed Tiffany's mismanagement during the pandemic and claimed that it was "burning cash and reporting losses".[[50]](#cite_note-51) In late October 2020, Tiffany and LVMH agreed to the original takeover plan, though at a slightly reduced price of nearly $16 billion, a minor reduction of 2.6% from the aforementioned deal. The new deal reduced the amount paid per share by LVMH from the original price of $135 to $131.50.[[51]](#cite_note-52) LVMH completed the purchase of Tiffany in January 2021.[[52]](#cite_note-53)

Under Arnault's leadership, LVMH has grown to become the largest company by market capitalization in the [eurozone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurozone "Eurozone"),[[53]](#cite_note-54) with a record of 313 billion euros ($382 billion) as of May 2021.[[54]](#cite_note-55) Arnault has promoted decisions toward decentralizing the group's brands as a business strategy. As a result of these measures, brands under the LVMH umbrella such as Tiffany are still viewed as independent firms with their history.[[20]](#cite_note-:3-21)

Arnault has said that brands like Louis Vuitton and Dior are successful because "they have these two aspects, which may be contradictory: They are timeless, [and] they are at the utmost level of modernity."[[55]](#cite_note-forbesindia-56)

In November 2024, the Arnault family acquired a majority ownership stake in French [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football") club [Paris FC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_FC "Paris FC"), which was then playing in [Ligue 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ligue_2 "Ligue 2"), the second tier of the French football system.[[56]](#cite_note-57)[[57]](#cite_note-58) Later that season, the club achieved promotion to [Ligue 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ligue_1 "Ligue 1") for the first time in 46 years.[[58]](#cite_note-59)

## Personal life

### Family

In 1973, Arnault married Anne Dewavrin. Together, they had two children, [Delphine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delphine_Arnault "Delphine Arnault") and [Antoine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoine_Arnault "Antoine Arnault").[[9]](#cite_note-France24-10) They separated in 1990.[[59]](#cite_note-Business_Insider-60) In 1991, he married [Hélène Mercier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hélène_Mercier-Arnault "Hélène Mercier-Arnault"), a Canadian-born concert pianist. They have three sons, Alexandre, [Frédéric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frédéric_Arnault "Frédéric Arnault"), and Jean. Arnault and Mercier live in Paris.[[59]](#cite_note-Business_Insider-60) Arnault has four grandchildren, two from his son Antoine and two from his daughter, Delphine.[[60]](#cite_note-61)

All five children—Delphine, Antoine, Alexandre, Frédéric, and Jean—have official roles in brands controlled by Arnault, along with his niece Stephanie Watine Arnault.[[61]](#cite_note-62) Alexandre is the EVP of Tiffany & Co., Frédéric is the CEO of LVMH Watches,[[62]](#cite_note-63) and Jean is the Director of Watchmaking Marketing and Development at Louis Vuitton.[[63]](#cite_note-64) Since 2010, Arnault's daughter Delphine has been with [Xavier Niel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Niel "Xavier Niel"), a French billionaire businessman active in the telecommunications and technology industry. Effective February 1, 2023, Delphine is the chief executive officer of the luxury brand Dior.[[64]](#cite_note-65)

### Wealth

In April 1999, Arnault was first considered to be the richest person in fashion, topping [Zara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zara_(retailer) "Zara (retailer)")'s [Amancio Ortega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amancio_Ortega "Amancio Ortega").[[65]](#cite_note-66) That same year, he set up Pilinvest (Pilinvest Participations and Pilinvest Investissements),[[66]](#cite_note-67) a holding company based in Belgium.[[67]](#cite_note-68) Through Pilinvest, Arnault has been holding an 81% stake in Agache (former Groupe Arnault), the holding company that owns 48% of LVMH and 63% of its voting rights. In 2008, he established Protectinvest, a private foundation in Belgium set up to safeguard the integrity of the LVMH group until 2023; the foundation locked up the Arnault children's ability to sell shares in Pilinvest until 2023, by which time Arnault's youngest child turned 25, an age deemed old enough to assume responsibility for LVMH.[[68]](#cite_note-69)

In December 2011, six months before Socialist [François Hollande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/François_Hollande "François Hollande") took office as [President of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_France "President of France"), he transferred a 31 percent stake in Groupe Arnault – at the time considered by the newspaper *[Libération](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libération "Libération")* worth €6.5 billion – to Pilinvest.[[69]](#cite_note-70)[[70]](#cite_note-71)

In 2016, Arnault was paid €7.8 million as the CEO of the LVMH group.[[71]](#cite_note-72) In July 2019, Arnault became the second-richest man in the world, with a net worth of $103 billion.[[72]](#cite_note-73) Arnault briefly surpassed [Jeff Bezos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Bezos "Jeff Bezos") to become the richest person in the world in December 2019,[[73]](#cite_note-74) and again for a short time in January 2020.[[74]](#cite_note-75) During the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), Arnault saw his wealth shrink by $30 billion as sales of luxury goods plummeted.[[75]](#cite_note-76)

On 5 August 2021, Arnault regained the status of the wealthiest man in the world, with his net worth climbing to $198.4 billion. This occurred as sales of [LVMH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LVMH "LVMH")'s luxury goods surged in China and other parts of Asia.[[76]](#cite_note-77)[[77]](#cite_note-78) He is listed as "Bernard Arnault & family" on the Forbes Billionaires list.[[78]](#cite_note-:1-79) *[Forbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbes "Forbes")* estimated the Bernard Arnault & family fortune to be $158 billion in 2022, positioning him ahead of [Bill Gates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Gates "Bill Gates").[[78]](#cite_note-:1-79) In 2022, Arnault changed the legal structure of Agache from a [Societas Europaea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Societas_Europaea "Societas Europaea") (SE) to a joint-stock partnership to ensure family control over LVMH in the long term.[[79]](#cite_note-80)

Arnault and his family had an estimated peak net worth of [US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_dollar "United States dollar")240.7 billion in April 2023, according to *[Forbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbes "Forbes")*.[[80]](#cite_note-81) This made him the richest person in the world at the time, surpassing [Elon Musk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elon_Musk "Elon Musk"). Musk would surpass Arnault in June 2023 in net worth with $240 billion, as Arnault's wealth dropped to $190 billion.

According to *Bloomberg Billionaires Index* Arnault was the wealthiest person in the world, with a net worth of about US $218 billion in May 2024.[[81]](#cite_note-82) By 14 June 2024, according to *Forbes*, Musk had regained first place, with Bezos in second place, and Arnault, with [US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_dollar "United States dollar")194.2 billion, in third place.[[82]](#cite_note-83)

### Request for Belgian citizenship

In 2013, it was disclosed that Arnault planned to apply for [Belgian citizenship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgian_citizenship "Belgian citizenship") and was considering moving to Belgium.[[83]](#cite_note-84) In April 2013, Arnault said that he had been misquoted and that he never intended to leave France: "I repeatedly said that I would stay as a resident in France and that I would continue to pay my taxes... Today, I decided to remove any ambiguity. I withdraw my request for Belgian nationality. Requesting Belgian nationality was to better protect the foundation that I created with the sole purpose of ensuring the continuity and integrity of the LVMH group if I were to die."[[84]](#cite_note-85)

On 10 April 2013, Arnault announced he had decided to abandon his application for Belgian citizenship, saying he did not want the move to be misinterpreted as a measure of tax evasion, at a time when France faced economic and social challenges.[[85]](#cite_note-86) Arnault also stated several employees requested to leave France for tax purposes but he declined their requests, explaining "the 75% tax would not raise a lot of revenue but should prove less divisive, as now it was set to be levied on firms rather than people, and only due to stay in place for two years."[[86]](#cite_note-87)

### Transport

Arnault owned the 70 m (230 ft) converted research vessel [*Amadeus*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jade_Yachts "Jade Yachts"), which was sold in late 2015.[[87]](#cite_note-88) His current 101.5 m (333 ft) yacht [*Symphony*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_(yacht) "Symphony (yacht)") was built in the Netherlands by [Feadship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feadship "Feadship").[[88]](#cite_note-89)

In October 2022, Arnault stated that LVMH sold its private jet after a Twitter user began to track its flights and stated he began renting private aircraft for his personal and business flights instead.[[89]](#cite_note-90) The aircraft was a [Bombardier Global 7500](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombardier_Global_7500 "Bombardier Global 7500") which was registered F-GVMA.[[90]](#cite_note-91)

### Lifestyle

Arnault plays tennis weekly, watches his weight, and works continually.[[55]](#cite_note-forbesindia-56)

## Art collection

Arnault's collection includes works by [Picasso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picasso "Picasso"), [Yves Klein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yves_Klein "Yves Klein"), [Henry Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Moore "Henry Moore"), and [Andy Warhol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Warhol "Andy Warhol").[[91]](#cite_note-92)[[92]](#cite_note-93) He was also instrumental in establishing [LVMH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LVMH "LVMH") as a significant patron of art in France.[[93]](#cite_note-94) The LVMH Young Fashion Designer was created as an international competition open to students from fine arts schools. Every year, the winner is awarded a grant to support the creation of the designer's label and a year of mentorship.[[94]](#cite_note-95)[[95]](#cite_note-96)

From 1999 to 2003, he owned [Phillips de Pury & Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phillips_de_Pury_&_Company "Phillips de Pury & Company"), an art [auction house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auction_house "Auction house"), and bought out the first French auctioneer, Tajan.[[96]](#cite_note-97)[[97]](#cite_note-98) In 2006, Arnault started the building project of the [Louis Vuitton Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Vuitton_Foundation "Louis Vuitton Foundation"). Dedicated to the creation and contemporary art, the building was designed by the architect [Frank Gehry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry "Frank Gehry").[[98]](#cite_note-99) The Foundation's grand opening at the [Jardin d'Acclimatation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jardin_d'Acclimatation "Jardin d'Acclimatation") Paris was held on 20 October 2014.[[99]](#cite_note-100)

## Political views

In the second round of the [2017 French presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_French_presidential_election "2017 French presidential election"), Arnault publicly supported [Emmanuel Macron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmanuel_Macron "Emmanuel Macron").[[100]](#cite_note-101) Macron's wife, [Brigitte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigitte_Macron "Brigitte Macron"), was the French teacher of Arnault's sons Frédéric and Jean when they were students at the [Lycée Saint-Louis-de-Gonzague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lycée_Saint-Louis-de-Gonzague "Lycée Saint-Louis-de-Gonzague").[[101]](#cite_note-102) In 2025, he attended the [second inauguration of Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_inauguration_of_Donald_Trump "Second inauguration of Donald Trump").[[102]](#cite_note-103)

Arnault said that [Gabriel Zucman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel_Zucman "Gabriel Zucman") was a "far-left activist" who wanted to "destroy the French economy".[[103]](#cite_note-104)

## Awards and honors

* Grand Officer of the [Order of Merit of the Italian Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Merit_of_the_Italian_Republic "Order of Merit of the Italian Republic") (Italy, 2006)[[104]](#cite_note-105)
* Commandeur of the [Ordre des Arts et des Lettres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordre_des_Arts_et_des_Lettres "Ordre des Arts et des Lettres") (France, 2011)[[105]](#cite_note-106)
* [The Woodrow Wilson Award for Global Corporate Citizenship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Woodrow_Wilson_Award_for_Global_Corporate_Citizenship "The Woodrow Wilson Award for Global Corporate Citizenship") (2011)[[106]](#cite_note-107)
* Honorary Knight Commander of the Most Excellent [Order of the British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_British_Empire "Order of the British Empire") (UK, 2012)[[107]](#cite_note-108)
* The [Museum of Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Modern_Art "Museum of Modern Art")'s David Rockefeller Award (March 2014)[[108]](#cite_note-Bernard_Arnault_to_Be_Honored_at_MoMA_Luncheon-109)[[109]](#cite_note-Bernard_Arnault_Receives_MoMa's_David_Rockefeller_Award-110)
* [Medal of Pushkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Pushkin "Medal of Pushkin") (Russia, 2017)[[110]](#cite_note-111)
* Grand Cross of the [Légion d'honneur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legion_of_Honour "Legion of Honour") (France, 31 December 2023)[[111]](#cite_note-112)[[1]](#cite_note-GC-1)
* Member of the political economics, statistics and finances section of the [Académie des Sciences Morales et Politiques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Académie_des_Sciences_Morales_et_Politiques "Académie des Sciences Morales et Politiques") (France, 2024)[[112]](#cite_note-113)[[113]](#cite_note-114)[[114]](#cite_note-115)

args.summary:
This is the Wikipedia article on Bernard Arnault, the French billionaire businessman and chairman/CEO of LVMH, the world's largest luxury goods company.

**Background and Early Life:**
- Born Bernard Jean Étienne Arnault on March 5, 1949, in Roubaix, France, to a manufacturing family. Raised in a devoutly Catholic household, he studied civil engineering and mathematics at École Polytechnique, graduating in 1971. He began his career at his father's company, Ferret-Savinel, shifting its focus to real estate.

**Career Timeline:**
- 1984: Acquired the struggling textile/retail conglomerate Boussac Saint-Frères (which owned Christian Dior) for a ceremonial one franc, laying off 9,000 workers in two years and earning the nickname "The Terminator." By 1987, the company was profitable with $112 million in earnings on $1.9 billion in revenue.
- 1987-1989: Co-founded LVMH (Louis Vuitton Moët Hennessy) with Alain Chevalier and Henry Racamier. Through a series of strategic share purchases (totaling ~43.5% of shares by January 1989), he gained control and ousted Racamier, becoming chairman of the executive management board on January 13, 1989.
- 1989-2001: Led aggressive expansion, acquiring brands including Céline (1988), Berluti and Kenzo (1993), Guerlain (1994), Loewe (1996), Marc Jacobs and Sephora (1997), Thomas Pink (1999), Emilio Pucci (2000), and Fendi, DKNY, and La Samaritaine (2001). Annual sales and profit rose five-fold in eleven years; market value increased 15-fold. Notable Gucci takeover battle in 1999 resulted in a $700 million profit for LVMH after settlement in 2001. Also invested in web companies (Boo.com, Netflix in 1999) via Europatweb.
- Since 2001: Acquired Princess Yachts (2008), Bulgari (2011, $5.2 billion), integrated full Christian Dior brand (2017), and acquired Tiffany & Co. (completed January 2021, ~$16 billion after a contentious negotiation involving cancelled deal and lawsuits). Record sales of €42.6 billion in 2017. LVMH became the largest company by market capitalization in the eurozone (313 billion euros as of May 2021). In November 2024, the Arnault family acquired a majority stake in French football club Paris FC, which achieved promotion to Ligue 1.

**Wealth:**
- One of the richest individuals in the world. As of December 2025, estimated net worth of US$190.4 billion (Forbes) and US$203 billion (Bloomberg Billionaires Index). He has periodically held the title of world's richest person (briefly surpassing Jeff Bezos in December 2019, again in August 2021 at $198.4 billion, and in April 2023 with a peak of $240.7 billion before being surpassed by Elon Musk). Uses holding structures including Pilinvest (Belgium) and Agache to control LVMH.

**Personal Life:**
- Married Anne Dewavrin (1978-1990, two children: Delphine and Antoine) and Hélène Mercier, a Canadian concert pianist (1991-present, three sons: Alexandre, Frédéric, and Jean). All five children hold roles in Arnault-controlled brands. Delphine became CEO of Dior in February 2023.

**Other Notable Facts:**
- Donated €200 million to the Notre-Dame fire rebuilding efforts (2019).
- Withdrew his application for Belgian citizenship in April 2013 after controversy.
- Art collection includes works by Picasso, Yves Klein, Henry Moore, and Andy Warhol. Founded the Louis Vuitton Foundation (designed by Frank Gehry, opened 2014).
- Political views: publicly supported Emmanuel Macron in 2017; attended Donald Trump's second inauguration in 2025.
- Awards include Grand Cross of the Légion d'honneur (2023), Honorary KBE (2012), and Commandeur of the Ordre des Arts et des Lettres (2011).

![](/media/Project/sbg/sbg/images/ir/financials/annual_reports/2026/message/son/son_pic01_sp.jpg)

Leading ASI's Four Key Areas to Become  
the No. 1 Platform Provider

Representative Director, Corporate Officer,  
Chairman & CEO  
SoftBank Group Corp.

Masayoshi Son

## AI is evolving toward Superintelligence

The evolution of AI is truly remarkable. I myself ask ChatGPT questions many times each day, using it as a sounding board for ideas and to deepen discussions with my colleagues. However, the evolution of AI is not limited to these conversations. AI is now evolving into AI agents that think and act autonomously, working day and night to advance the goals we give them.

Beyond even agentic AI, lies the era of ASI (Artificial Superintelligence), when AI will far surpass human intelligence. ASI cannot just be high intelligence. It must be high intelligence that supports the evolution of humanity and operates in harmony with human reason and morality to better the lives of all people. I believe we should understand ASI not simply as Superintelligence with superior cognitive ability, but as Superintelligence in a broader, more human-centered sense, guided by wisdom. We aim to become the No. 1 Platform Provider for this new era of ASI.

## Updating my 50-year life plan: bringing ASI to life in my 70s

When I was 19 and still in university, I drew up a 50-year life plan for myself as an entrepreneur: establish myself in my 20s, build a war chest in my 30s, take on major challenges in my 40s, achieve my vision in my 50s, and hand over the business to the next generation in my 60s.

I have stated this was my path many times and followed this 50-year life plan for many years. But now, at the age of 68, I find myself wanting to do more. I believe I have more to give to the growth of SBG and can continue working hard for another 10 or 15 years. With that in mind, I have decided to update my 50-year life plan to continue taking on challenges into my 70s. That challenge is bringing ASI to life. If I am going to achieve this, I cannot settle for anything less than leading the Group to be No. 1 in this powerful technology. I want us to become the undisputed No. 1 ASI Platform Provider in Japan, and in the world.

## The next 30-year vision is becoming reality

Humanity has continued to evolve over its roughly 300,000-year history. Over that time, our intelligence and ability to perform have been both our greatest strengths and the cause of our most acute limitations. With ASI, we will be able to overcome our limits and evolve further.

In 2010, at the 30th anniversary of our founding, we announced SoftBank’s Next 30-Year Vision. In it, we envisioned a future in which computers can learn and think on their own and connect to robots. What we described at the time as a “brain computer” is precisely what is now called ASI. We are now witnessing AI evolving into intelligence that surpasses that of humans, and that intelligence taking on the body of a robot and beginning to operate in the real world. The future we described in the Next 30-Year Vision is now becoming a reality before our eyes.

To be clear, I do not believe ASI will replace humans. ASI is powerful—but it is a tool, a colleague, and a partner in our evolution. It is something that will help us evolve. In education, it will serve as a tutor, helping advance each student’s learning experience. In research, it will become a diligent and capable assistant. In healthcare, it will support each patient through treatment and offer guidance tailored to their individual needs. And when ASI connects to robots, it will become physical ASI—intelligence with a physical manifestation—an entity that moves, works, and acts on its own in the real world. In dangerous areas—such as space, deep water, and disaster sites—and in physically challenging jobs—such as manufacturing, construction, and agriculture—these intelligent robots will help make our lives easier and advance humanity’s progress.

## Securing the four corners essential to realizing ASI

To bring this future to life, we need frontier AI models that generate intelligence in ASI, semiconductors that handle the enormous computing power required to run such models, AI infrastructure that integrates and operates those technologies, and robots that enable AI to work in the real world. We have prioritized these as our key focus areas and have made concerted efforts to position ourselves as a leader in each.

Our key partner in the AI model area, which governs intelligence, is OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT. Its products have rapidly expanded from chatting to image generation, video generation, coding, and cybersecurity.

In semiconductors, Arm is becoming even more important. In the first phase of the AI evolution, which included conversations and image and video generation, GPUs that excelled at parallel computation played a major role. In the second phase, in which AI agents will take on active roles, CPUs that support complex processing and run entire systems will become a cornerstone of AI development. Arm has overwhelming strength in semiconductor design intellectual property, the core technology for CPUs. Furthermore, Arm has expanded its established IP business to include developing and selling chips. \*1

![](/media/Project/sbg/sbg/images/ir/financials/annual_reports/2026/message/son/pic_01_en.png)

At the core of the AI infrastructure are data centers and power. Enormous AI data centers and a substantial power supply are required to operate and keep the servers, which contain vast numbers of semiconductors, running continuously at scale and with stability. For this reason, in March of this year, we announced a public-private partnership project to develop a site in the U.S. state of Ohio that includes both 10 GW of power generation facilities and a 10 GW AI data center.\*2 In May, we also announced that we would develop and operate an AI data center with 5 GW of capacity in France.\*3

We are also making steady progress in robotics. Our portfolio includes numerous robotics companies with leading expertise across various fields. In October 2025, we also announced plans to acquire ABB’s robotics business, a global leader in industrial robotics.\*4 Once ASI is embedded into robots, we will have entities that can think, make judgments, and work independently and collaboratively.

In the board game Othello, the outcome is not determined solely by the number of pieces on the board early in the game. Once you secure the four corners in the middle of the game, the position can turn quickly in your favor. In the same way, the fact that we are moving toward securing the four key areas—the four corners of ASI—gives us a major advantage as we aim to become the No. 1 ASI Platform Provider.

* \*1 See Arm’s press release “Arm Announces AGI CPU: Silicon Foundation for the Cloud in the Agentic AI Era” dated March 25, 2026.
* \*2 See the U.S. Department of Energy press release “Energy Department Announces Partnership to Ensure Affordable Energy and Power America’s AI Future” dated March 20, 2026.
* \*3 See SBG’s press release “[SoftBank Group to Build 5 GW of AI Data Center Capacity in France](/en/news/press/20260531_0)” dated May 31, 2026.
* \*4 See SBG’s press release “[Acquisition of ABB Ltd’s Robotics Business](/en/news/press/20251008)” dated October 8, 2025. The acquisition is expected to close in late 2026.

## Aiming for NAV of ¥1 quadrillion in 2042

SBG is a strategic investment holding company. In addition to subsidiaries such as Arm and SoftBank, we hold shares in portfolio companies such as OpenAI and ByteDance. The NAV (Net Asset Value), which is calculated by subtracting net interest-bearing debt from the value of these equity holdings, has now reached ¥74 trillion (as of June 23, 2026).\*5 This is twice as much as SBG’s market capitalization of ¥37 trillion as of the same date. In other words, the value of our equity holdings is still not fully reflected in our share price.

I have previously compared SBG to a goose that lays golden eggs. If each golden egg represents ¥1 trillion, in 2010 when NAV was ¥3 trillion, it would be three golden eggs. Over the last 16 years, this increased to ¥74 trillion in 2026, or 74 golden eggs.

![](/media/Project/sbg/sbg/images/ir/financials/annual_reports/2026/message/son/pic_02_en.png)

* \* The chart shows NAV at each quarter-end (before tax and after deduction of asset-backed financing). However, market capitalization is shown through the end of March 1999, and NAV is shown from the end of June 1999 onward. The ¥200 billion figure for 1994 is market capitalization as of September 30, 1994, after SBG’s listing. The ¥3 trillion figure for 2010 is NAV as of March 31, 2010, before the announcement of the Next 30-Year Vision. Multiples were calculated based on the approximate figures shown on this chart.

For years, SBG has identified and invested in the core technologies of the Information Revolution as they evolve with the times. Through our unique organizational strategy, the Cluster of No. 1 Strategy, we have generated synergies and grown a wide range of Group companies and investees. Eggs do not lay eggs. Only the goose does. In other words, SBG is that goose: one that has continued to increase the number of eggs it lays, and whose value far exceeds the sum of the eggs visible today.

Now that we have passed the halfway point of the Next 30-Year Vision, I want us to take on another major challenge over the next 16 years. NAV grew 15X in the 16 years from 1994 to 2010, and 25X in the 16 years from 2010 to 2026. From here, over the same 16-year period, we aim to realize a NAV of ¥1 quadrillion in 2042 (see chart). This is not something we can achieve simply by adding up the golden eggs that are already visible. We are moving towards this future by securing our leadership position in the four key areas and by continuing to nurture businesses and portfolio companies that will become future golden eggs, through our Cluster of No. 1 Strategy.

* \*5 NAV as of June 23, 2026: Calculated by making the following adjustments to NAV as of the end of March 2026. Share prices: closing prices on June 23, 2026 for Arm, SoftBank Corp., T-Mobile, and Intel. FX rate: $1 = ¥161.63 (as of June 23, 2026).

## The AI revolution has only just begun

Some people say there is an AI bubble. I disagree. The AI revolution has only just begun. The current evolution of AI resembles the early days of the internet. At that time, people also questioned whether it was merely a passing trend or overvalued. But afterward, tech companies such as Amazon, Google, and Microsoft went on to grow significantly and reshaped the very structure of industries around the world.

If a person had the opportunity to travel back in time, I have no doubt that investing in those tech companies would be one of the first things they would do. The same thing is about to happen now with AI. AI is not just a single technology. It will transform every industry and dramatically expand the potential of human intelligence and execution. Its significance may even surpass the impact of the internet and smartphones.

That is why we must take on this challenge now. Decades from now, people will say, “That was the beginning of the ASI era.” We are determined to stand at the center of that era, look ahead and build toward the future.

## For the happiness of everyone

Our overarching goal is not just to increase the value of our company. It is to realize, in an even greater form in the ASI era, our founding corporate philosophy: “Information Revolution—Happiness for everyone.”

ASI will expand the limits of human intelligence, while physical ASI will dramatically expand the scope of human activity. Opportunities for education will increase, the quality of healthcare will improve, people will be freed from dangerous jobs and grueling work, and new inventions and industries will emerge. If ASI is used in the right way, humanity will become richer, freer, and happier.

That is exactly why ASI must not be defined by cognitive capability alone, but in a fuller sense, guided by wisdom. Our mission is to spread, as a foundation for society, not only high intelligence but a higher intelligence that creates happiness for people and operates in harmony with human reason and morality.

Two and a half years ago, I was at my father’s side in his final moments. I often still recall the words he left me with: “When a tiger dies, it leaves behind its skin; when people die, they leave behind their names.” When I was a child, my father would come home from work, have a drink, sit me on his lap, and tell me, “Do not live your life for money. Live your life to make people happy.” I carry his words and teachings with me as I continue to drive our mission forward. We aim for a NAV of ¥1 quadrillion, but this is not about pursuing money. If it were, my father would scold me. What I am pursuing is a future in which we can bring happiness to more people.

As we evolve into the No. 1 ASI Platform Provider, we will augment human intelligence, further our ability to execute, and expand what is possible for humanity. Bringing happiness to as many people as possible through this endeavor is the very realization of our corporate philosophy: “Information Revolution—Happiness for everyone.”

June 24, 2026  
SoftBank Group Corp.  
Representative Director, Corporate Officer, Chairman & CEO  
Masayoshi Son

**Masayoshi Son** ([Japanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_language "Japanese language"): 孫 正義; born **Masayoshi Yasumoto**, August 11, 1957) is a Japanese entrepreneur, investor, and philanthropist. A [Zainichi Korean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koreans_in_Japan "Koreans in Japan"), he is the founder, chairman and chief executive of [SoftBank Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SoftBank_Group "SoftBank Group") (SBG),[[2]](#cite_note-2) a technology-focused [investment holding company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Investment_company "Investment company"), as well as chairman of UK-based [Arm Holdings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arm_Ltd. "Arm Ltd.") and US-based [Stargate LLC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stargate_LLC "Stargate LLC").

As an entrepreneur, he achieved notability in software distribution, computing-related book and magazine publishing, and telecommunications in Japan, starting in the 1980s and booming throughout the 1990s and 2000s.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4) His early $20 million investment in [Alibaba Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alibaba_Group "Alibaba Group") in 2000 grew substantially over the years, reaching a valuation of around $75 billion by 2014 following Alibaba's [IPO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_public_offering "Initial public offering"), and contributing significantly to SoftBank's financial success.[[5]](#cite_note-5) SoftBank's 27 percent stake in Alibaba was worth $132 billion in 2018,[[6]](#cite_note-6) including additional purchases of the stock since 2000.[[7]](#cite_note-7)[[8]](#cite_note-8) The morphing of his own telecom company SoftBank Corp. into an [investment management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Investment_management "Investment management") firm called SoftBank Group Corp. made him noted worldwide as a [stock investor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stock_investor "Stock investor"). He is known for his bold investment strategies,[[9]](#cite_note-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10) sometimes resulting in major losses, particularly with the first and second [SoftBank Vision Funds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SoftBank_Vision_Fund "SoftBank Vision Fund").[[11]](#cite_note-11)[[12]](#cite_note-12)[[13]](#cite_note-13)

In 2013, Son was placed 45th on the [*Forbes* magazine's list of the World's Most Powerful People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbes_list_of_the_World's_Most_Powerful_People "Forbes list of the World's Most Powerful People").[[14]](#cite_note-14) In 2017 he was named Entrepreneur of the Year at [The Asian Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Asian_Awards "The Asian Awards"). As of May 2025, Son ranks 65th on the *Forbes*'s list of [The World's Billionaires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_World's_Billionaires "The World's Billionaires")[[15]](#cite_note-15) and is No. 177 on the *[Bloomberg Billionaires Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomberg_Billionaires_Index "Bloomberg Billionaires Index")*.[[16]](#cite_note-16) He had for many years the distinction of being the person who had [lost the most money in history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_largest_losses_of_wealth "List of largest losses of wealth") (more than $59 billion[[17]](#cite_note-17) during the [dot-com crash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dot-com_crash "Dot-com crash") of 2000 alone, when his SoftBank shares plummeted),[[18]](#cite_note-18) a feat surpassed by [Elon Musk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elon_Musk "Elon Musk")[[19]](#cite_note-19)[[20]](#cite_note-20)[[21]](#cite_note-21) in the following decades.

## Early life and education

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Masayoshi_Son&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Masayoshi Son was born Masayoshi Yasumoto[[22]](#cite_note-:3-22)[[23]](#cite_note-23) on August 11, 1957, in [Tosu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tosu,_Saga "Tosu, Saga"), [Saga Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saga_Prefecture "Saga Prefecture") to [Zainichi Korean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koreans_in_Japan "Koreans in Japan") parents.[[24]](#cite_note-24)[[25]](#cite_note-:0-25)[[26]](#cite_note-Martin-2019-26)[[27]](#cite_note-27) Son's grandfather, Son Jong-kyung, a native of [Daegu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daegu "Daegu"), moved to Japan during the [Japanese colonial period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korea_under_Japanese_rule "Korea under Japanese rule") where he worked as a miner.[[28]](#cite_note-:2-28) Son's father, Son Sam-heon, raised pigs and chickens, and illegally built the family home on land that was owned by the [Japanese National Railways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_National_Railways "Japanese National Railways"), which caused them trouble with the authorities.[[29]](#cite_note-auto1-29) His father started an illegal [sake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sake "Sake") business that eventually became successful enough for his family to become the first people in town to own a car.[[29]](#cite_note-auto1-29) His family eventually moved out of the neighborhood so that Son could attend a better school.[[29]](#cite_note-auto1-29) Throughout his childhood, Son's family refrained from using their Korean names.[[22]](#cite_note-:3-22) He did however experience [bullying and discrimination for his Korean origin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Korean_sentiment_in_Japan "Anti-Korean sentiment in Japan") and at one point contemplated suicide.[[30]](#cite_note-:4-30)

Son idolized businessman [Den Fujita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Den_Fujita "Den Fujita"), the founder of [McDonald's Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McDonald's "McDonald's"), and attempted to contact him multiple times to no avail. This culminated in Son purchasing a plane ticket to [Tokyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo "Tokyo") and making an unsolicited appearance at the headquarters of McDonald's Japan, where he was able to speak to Fujita for 15 minutes. Fujita advised Son to begin studying [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_studies "English studies") as well as [computer science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_science "Computer science"), and to move to the United States for education.[[28]](#cite_note-:2-28)[[31]](#cite_note-31)[[32]](#cite_note-32) Following this advice, Son dropped out of high school in Japan and, at the age of 16,[[30]](#cite_note-:4-30) moved to [Oakland, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oakland,_California "Oakland, California"). He studied English at [Holy Names College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Names_University "Holy Names University") and graduated from high school in three weeks after attending [Serramonte High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serramonte_High_School "Serramonte High School").[[33]](#cite_note-33) He subsequently enrolled at the [University of California, Berkeley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Berkeley "University of California, Berkeley"), where he studied [economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economics "Economics"), graduating in 1980.[[34]](#cite_note-34)[[35]](#cite_note-35)

He began his first business endeavours while still a student. With the help of some professors including [Forrest Mozer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forrest_Mozer "Forrest Mozer"), Son created an electronic translator that he sold to [Sharp Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharp_Corporation "Sharp Corporation") for $1.7 million. He made another $1.5 million by importing used video game machines from Japan, on credit and installing them in dormitories and restaurants.[[25]](#cite_note-:0-25) He also started a video game company called Unison World in Oakland; he sold the company to an associate for $2 million, and the company was later acquired by [Kyocera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyocera "Kyocera").[[36]](#cite_note-36)

Following his return to Japan, he decided to adopt his Korean surname Son for professional purposes instead of his family's Japanese surname Yasumoto.[[25]](#cite_note-:0-25)[[37]](#cite_note-auto-37)[[29]](#cite_note-auto1-29)[[30]](#cite_note-:4-30) He encountered pushback from some of his relatives who feared to be exposed as Korean.[[30]](#cite_note-:4-30) For this action and other similar ones, Son is considered to be a role model for ethnic Korean children in Japan.[[38]](#cite_note-Korean_name-38)

## Career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Masayoshi_Son&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### SoftBank

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Masayoshi_Son&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: SoftBank")]

Son is the founder, CEO and largest shareholder of SoftBank; as of December 2022, he had a 34.2 per cent stake in the company.[[39]](#cite_note-39) He founded the company in 1981 as a software distributor and a publisher of computer-related literature.

### SoftBank Corp.

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Masayoshi_Son&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: SoftBank Corp.")]

Son was the CEO of SoftBank Corp., the mobile business of [SoftBank Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SoftBank_Group "SoftBank Group"), until 2021.[[40]](#cite_note-40)

### Yahoo! and Alibaba

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Masayoshi_Son&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Yahoo! and Alibaba")]

Son was an early investor in internet firms, buying a share of [Yahoo!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yahoo! "Yahoo!") in 1995 and investing a $20 million stake into [Alibaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alibaba_Group "Alibaba Group") in 1999; he was briefly the richest person in the world before the stock market crashed.[[41]](#cite_note-WSJ_2022-08-41) Son's holding company [SoftBank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SoftBank "SoftBank") owned 29.5% of [Alibaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alibaba_Group "Alibaba Group"), which was worth around $108.7 billion as of 23 October 2018.[[42]](#cite_note-:1-42)[[43]](#cite_note-43)[[44]](#cite_note-44) Although SoftBank's stake in Yahoo! had dwindled to 7%, Son established Yahoo! BroadBand in September 2001 with [Yahoo! Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yahoo!_Japan "Yahoo! Japan") in which he still owned a controlling interest. After a severe devaluation of SoftBank's equity, Son was forced to focus his attention on Yahoo! BB and BB Phone. So far, SoftBank has accumulated about $1.3 billion in debt. Yet, Yahoo! BB acquired [Japan Telecom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_Telecom "Japan Telecom"), the then third largest broadband and landline provider with 600,000 residential and 170,000 commercial subscribers. Yahoo! BB is now Japan's leading broadband provider.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] In June 2020, Son stepped down from the Alibaba board.[[45]](#cite_note-45) By 2023, SoftBank had sold most of its Alibaba stake.[[46]](#cite_note-46)

### Arm Holdings

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Masayoshi_Son&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Arm Holdings")]

In July 2016, immediately following the UK's [Brexit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brexit "Brexit") referendum, SoftBank announced plans to acquire [Arm Holdings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arm_Ltd. "Arm Ltd.") for £23.4 billion ($31.4 billion) which would be the largest ever purchase of a European technology company. In September 2016, SoftBank announced that the transaction was complete. The total acquisition price was approximately £24 billion ($34 billion).[[47]](#cite_note-47)[[42]](#cite_note-:1-42)

In 2020, SoftBank Group agreed to sell U.K. chip designer Arm Limited to U.S. chip-maker [Nvidia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nvidia "Nvidia") in a cash and stock deal initially worth $40 billion. The buy price, initially set at $40bn (cash and Nvidia shares) when first announced in September 2020, had risen closer to an estimated $66bn by 2022 given the intervening hike in Nvidia's stock – that would make this deal the biggest deal in the semiconductor market. Announcing the deal, SoftBank said the combination of Arm and Nvidia would create a computing company "that will lead the era" of [artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence").[[48]](#cite_note-48) However, the deal with Nvidia failed as announced in February 2022.[[49]](#cite_note-49)[[50]](#cite_note-50) After the collapse of the deal with Nvidia because of objections from [U.S.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") and [EU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") antitrust regulators, SoftBank Group Corp.'s chip maker Arm filed in 2023 with regulators confidentially for a U.S. stock market listing seeking to raise between $8 billion and $10 billion.[[51]](#cite_note-51) The estimated value of the UK chipmaker being listed by SoftBank at that date ranged from $30bn to $70bn.[[52]](#cite_note-52)

### Sprint Corporation

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Masayoshi_Son&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Sprint Corporation")]

In the 2010s, through his holdings in SoftBank, Son bought a 76% share in [Sprint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sprint_Corporation "Sprint Corporation"). SoftBank later accumulated further shares in Sprint to about 84% ownership.[[53]](#cite_note-53)[[54]](#cite_note-54)

[Sprint and T-Mobile US merged in 2020 in an all-shares deal for $26 billion.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merger_of_Sprint_Corporation_and_T-Mobile_US "Merger of Sprint Corporation and T-Mobile US") By 2021, SoftBank Group Corp. had acquired 4.5% of [Deutsche Telekom AG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deutsche_Telekom "Deutsche Telekom") (parent company of T-Mobile) and sold its stake in T-Mobile US Inc. to the German telecommunications carrier.[[55]](#cite_note-55)

### Solar power

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Masayoshi_Son&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Solar power")]

In response to the [Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fukushima_Daiichi_nuclear_disaster "Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster") in 2011, Masayoshi Son criticized the nuclear industry for creating "the problem that worries Japanese the most today"[[56]](#cite_note-56) and engaged in investing in a nationwide [solar power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_power "Solar power") network for Japan.[[57]](#cite_note-57) In March 2018, it was announced that Son was investing in the biggest ever solar project, a 200GW development planned for Saudi Arabia as part of its [Vision 2030](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Vision_2030 "Saudi Vision 2030").[[58]](#cite_note-58)

In July 2018, coverage indicated that Son "would underwrite most of 100 GW" of a planned 275 GW of new renewable provision in India by 2027.[[59]](#cite_note-59)

### Vision Fund

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Masayoshi_Son&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Vision Fund")]

Established in 2017, [SoftBank Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SoftBank_Group "SoftBank Group")'s investment vehicle, the $100 billion [Vision Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vision_Fund "Vision Fund"), was intended to invest in emerging technologies like artificial intelligence (AI), robotics and the [internet of things](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_of_things "Internet of things").[[60]](#cite_note-60) As of 2019, it aimed to nearly double its portfolio of AI companies from 70 to 125.[[61]](#cite_note-61) However, it also invested in companies supposedly focused on revolutionizing real estate, transportation, and retail. Son claimed he would make personal connections with the CEOs of all companies funded by Vision Fund in order to enhance the creation of intertwined synergies among those companies.[[62]](#cite_note-62)[[63]](#cite_note-63) Son planned to raise $100 billion for a new fund every few years, investing about $50 billion a year in startups.[[26]](#cite_note-Martin-2019-26) In 2019, a second Vision Fund was created with a target of $108 billion, of which $38 billion would come from SoftBank itself.[[64]](#cite_note-64) But the amount was scaled down due to lack of investing partners beyond SoftBank Group itself and Masayoshi Son.[[65]](#cite_note-65)[[66]](#cite_note-66)[[67]](#cite_note-67)

As of 2020, the first fund had invested in 88 companies including [Coupang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coupang "Coupang"),[[68]](#cite_note-68) [Didi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DiDi "DiDi"),[[69]](#cite_note-69) [Doordash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DoorDash "DoorDash"),[[70]](#cite_note-70) [Fanatics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fanatics_(sports_retailer) "Fanatics (sports retailer)"),[[71]](#cite_note-71) [Grab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grab_(company) "Grab (company)"),[[72]](#cite_note-72) [Oyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oyo_Rooms "Oyo Rooms"),[[73]](#cite_note-73) [Paytm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paytm "Paytm")[[74]](#cite_note-Masayoshi_Son-74) [Uber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uber "Uber"),[[75]](#cite_note-75) and [WeWork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WeWork "WeWork"),[[76]](#cite_note-76) but had experienced an awkward fall from grace[[77]](#cite_note-77)[[78]](#cite_note-78)[[79]](#cite_note-79)[[80]](#cite_note-80) as the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic") and a Chinese regulatory crackdown[[81]](#cite_note-81)[[82]](#cite_note-82) accelerated the exposure of the Japanese investment management conglomerate's portfolio weaknesses.[[83]](#cite_note-83) Son became noted as a [stock investor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stock_investor "Stock investor") after the meteoric rise of [Alibaba Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alibaba_Group "Alibaba Group"). He had invested $20 million in [Jack Ma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Ma "Jack Ma")'s Alibaba back in 2000 when it was a young Chinese [startup company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Startup_company "Startup company")[[84]](#cite_note-84) although regrettably passing up early opportunities to invest in both [Amazon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Inc. "Amazon Inc.") and [Tesla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tesla_Inc. "Tesla Inc.").[[85]](#cite_note-85) In addition, he raised his global profile as stock investor since starting SoftBank Vision Fund in 2017, creating an unprecedented investment vehicle of almost $100 billion to back technology startups. But by 2021, he was still struggling to persuade investors of the value of his efforts, in part because of major losses with companies such as [WeWork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WeWork "WeWork"), [OneWeb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OneWeb "OneWeb"), [Wirecard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wirecard "Wirecard"),[[86]](#cite_note-86) OYO Rooms, [Katerra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katerra "Katerra")[[87]](#cite_note-87) or [Greensill Capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greensill_Capital "Greensill Capital"), and SoftBank Group's own stock chronically traded far below the value of its assets reflecting a discount[[88]](#cite_note-88) associated with tax liabilities, risk, past performance, losses, performance fees and high probability of occurrence of several [haircuts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haircut_(finance) "Haircut (finance)") given Son's poor track record while running the Vision Fund[[89]](#cite_note-89) and high enthusiasm for investing vast sums in loss-making companies at eye-popping valuations.[[90]](#cite_note-90)[[91]](#cite_note-91)[[92]](#cite_note-92)[[93]](#cite_note-93)[[94]](#cite_note-94) By October 2021, Masayoshi Son had accelerated the pace of his startup investments quintupling the number of companies in his Vision Fund 2 portfolio in less than 9 months, SoftBank was cutting more deals with fewer staff than ever and the average investment amount per company had fallen from $943 million in Vision Fund 1 to $192 million in Vision Fund 2.[[95]](#cite_note-95)[[96]](#cite_note-96)[[97]](#cite_note-97) In 2022, SoftBank Vision Fund posted a record 3.5 trillion yen loss ($27.4 billion) for its financial year ended on 31 March 2022 as the valuation of its stock portfolio plummeted.[[98]](#cite_note-98) SoftBank's bad timing-prone, impulsive investment decisions regarding previously overhyped and consequently overvalued startups like [Klarna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klarna "Klarna"),[[99]](#cite_note-99)[[100]](#cite_note-100) had plunged in value while some other investment firms had even been able to cash in before the startups' comedown to reap hundreds of millions of dollars in profit.[[101]](#cite_note-101) In August 2022, Masayoshi Son said he was "embarrassed" and "ashamed" when asked to talk about the way he had run the SoftBank Vision Fund[[102]](#cite_note-102)[[103]](#cite_note-103) and *[Barron's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barron's_(newspaper) "Barron's (newspaper)")* characterized the fund as a "failed experiment"[[104]](#cite_note-104) while *[The Wall Street Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wall_Street_Journal "The Wall Street Journal")* called SoftBank a "big loser"[[41]](#cite_note-WSJ_2022-08-41) and *[Bloomberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomberg_News "Bloomberg News")* elaborated on "Masayoshi Son's broken business model".[[105]](#cite_note-105)

By November 2022, according to the *[Financial Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_Times "Financial Times")*, Masayoshi Son personally owed SoftBank $4.7bn because of growing losses on the Japanese conglomerate's technology bets, which have also rendered the value of his stake in the group's second Vision Fund worthless.[[106]](#cite_note-106) By February 2023, this personal debt totaled $5.1 billion according to *Bloomberg* calculations based on company disclosures. This debt on side deals he set up at SoftBank Group Corp. to boost his compensation, as losses mounted at its core Vision Fund venture capital arm*,* sparked controversy due to corporate governance concerns, but Son insisted that there was no [conflict of interest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conflict_of_interest "Conflict of interest").[[107]](#cite_note-107) As of March 2023, while the [collapse of Silicon Valley Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collapse_of_Silicon_Valley_Bank "Collapse of Silicon Valley Bank") was being investigated,[[108]](#cite_note-108) over a third of Son's SoftBank shares had been reportedly posted as collateral for margin loans and the Financial Times was recalling signs of an emergent doomsday scenario for both SoftBank Group and Masayoshi Son.[[109]](#cite_note-109)

### Stargate

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Masayoshi_Son&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Stargate")]

Son was named chairman of [The Stargate Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stargate_LLC "Stargate LLC"), an American artificial intelligence infrastructure joint venture formed by SoftBank, [OpenAI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OpenAI "OpenAI"), [Oracle Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oracle_Corporation "Oracle Corporation") and [MGX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MGX_(company) "MGX (company)"), in January 2025.[[110]](#cite_note-:5-110)

### Repositioning and AI-focused strategy (2023–2026)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Masayoshi_Son&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Repositioning and AI-focused strategy (2023–2026)")]

From 2023 onward, [SoftBank Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SoftBank_Group "SoftBank Group") announced a strategic shift toward artificial intelligence infrastructure and [semiconductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor "Semiconductor")-related investments. During this period, Son publicly stated that AI development would become the primary focus of the group’s future strategy. In 2024 and 2025, [SoftBank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SoftBank_Group "SoftBank Group") reported a return to profitability following earlier losses in the [Vision Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SoftBank_Vision_Fund "SoftBank Vision Fund") segment. [Reuters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reuters "Reuters") reported that SoftBank’s net profit for the second quarter of fiscal year 2025 more than doubled to ¥2.5 trillion, supported in part by valuation gains related to AI-linked technology holdings.[[111]](#cite_note-:6-111)

In January 2025, Son’s appointment as chairman of the artificial-intelligence infrastructure venture [Stargate LLC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stargate_LLC "Stargate LLC") aligned with this broader strategic shift.[[110]](#cite_note-:5-110) Analysts cited by Reuters noted that SoftBank’s increased emphasis on Arm Holdings, data centers and AI-related computing capacity was consistent with the strategic direction Son had outlined.[[112]](#cite_note-:7-112)

SoftBank also carried out several restructuring measures during this period, including consolidations and selective divestments, which the company said were intended to strengthen liquidity and align with its AI-oriented strategy.[[113]](#cite_note-:8-113)

Son was included in [*Time*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Magazine "Time Magazine")'s 100 Most Influential People in AI list in 2024.[[114]](#cite_note-114)

On June 2, 2026, SoftBank Group’s market value surpassed Toyota’s to rank first in Japan, propelling founder Masayoshi Son’s net worth to $100.7 billion on the *[Forbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbes "Forbes")* Real-Time Billionaires List. With this surge, he overtook Indian tycoon [Mukesh Ambani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mukesh_Ambani "Mukesh Ambani") to become Asia's richest person once again after more than a decade.[[115]](#cite_note-115) Just three days later, on June 4, as market enthusiasm cooled, his ranking quickly slipped back behind Mukesh Ambani and Adani.[[116]](#cite_note-116)

## Personal life

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Masayoshi_Son&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Son met his wife, Masami Ohno, the daughter of a prominent Japanese doctor, while both were students at the University of California, Berkeley.[[117]](#cite_note-117) They married in 1979 and have two daughters.[[118]](#cite_note-118) He lives in Tokyo in a three-story mansion that is valued at US$85 million and that has a golf range with technology to mimic the weather conditions and temperature of the world's top golf courses. He has also bought a home near Silicon Valley in [Woodside, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodside,_California "Woodside, California"), that cost him $117 million. He owns the [SoftBank Hawks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fukuoka_SoftBank_Hawks "Fukuoka SoftBank Hawks"), a professional Japanese baseball team.[[119]](#cite_note-119) Son has three brothers and is the second oldest of the siblings. His youngest brother, [Taizo Son](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taizo_Son "Taizo Son"), is a serial entrepreneur and investor, having founded [GungHo Online Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GungHo_Online_Entertainment "GungHo Online Entertainment") and the venture capital firm Mistletoe.[[120]](#cite_note-120) He is known for appreciating [Burgundy wine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgundy_wine "Burgundy wine"), in particular [*La Tche*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Tche_AOC "La Tche AOC") by [Domaine de la Romanée-Conti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domaine_de_la_Romanée-Conti "Domaine de la Romanée-Conti").[[121]](#cite_note-121)

When he went to the United States at 16 to attend high school and then the University of California, Berkeley, he decided to use his real Korean surname.[[37]](#cite_note-auto-37)[[29]](#cite_note-auto1-29) In an interview with *[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")*, Son stated that "If I had stayed all the time in Japan, I probably would have become much more conservative, just as other Japanese."[[29]](#cite_note-auto1-29)
