**Francesco Milleri** is the CEO of Luxottica and Chairman of EssilorLuxottica, as well as Chairman of Delfin. He graduated with honors in Law from the University of Florence, where he gained experience as a teaching assistant in Political Economy from 1984 to 1986. He then obtained an MBA in Business Administration with high merit from the Bocconi School of Management in Milan in 1987, followed by a two-year specialization in Corporate Finance at the Stern School of Business at New York University. In 1988, **Francesco Milleri** began his career as a business consultant for large Italian groups and multinational companies operating in various sectors, from mechanics to consumer goods, from financial institutions to pharmaceuticals. Alongside his consulting activities, he founded in 1996 and developed for about 20 years a group of companies focused on technology and systems for digital automation. He also sits on the Boards of Directors of the Leonardo Del Vecchio Foundation and IEO European Institute of Oncology. While maintaining responsibilities at Luxottica, **Francesco Milleri** has overseen the integration between Essilor and Luxottica since January 2017.

### Brand

**Luxottica Group** is an Italian company specialized in the production and trade of eyewear. It is present in over 150 countries across five continents and is the largest global manufacturer of frames for prescription glasses and sunglasses. The company was founded in Agordo in 1961 by Leonardo Del Vecchio.

Throughout its history, the company has distinguished itself through a wide range of acquisitions (notably that of the American brand Ray-Ban, a leader in the sunglasses sector previously owned by the multinational Bausch & Lomb). On March 24, 2014, **Luxottica** announced an agreement with Google for a new model of augmented reality glasses, a project revisited in 2023 with the Meta group.

In 2012, it was the first Italian company in the fashion sector by revenue. On January 16, 2017, the merger of Luxottica with the French group Essilor was announced. Since October 1, 2018, Luxottica Group S.p.A. has been a subsidiary of the holding EssilorLuxottica, which has held 100% of it since March 5, 2019.

The company was listed under the symbol LUX in the FTSE MIB index of the Milan Stock Exchange from 2000 to 2018.

args.summary:
This is a biographical profile page from the EssilorLuxottica corporate website about Francesco Milleri, who serves as Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of the company. 

Key biographical facts:
- Milleri is Chairman and CEO of EssilorLuxottica, a major eyewear corporation.
- He graduated with honors in Law from the University of Florence, where he worked as Assistant Professor of political economy from 1984 to 1986.
- He earned an MBA in Business Administration with high merit from Bocconi University in Milan in 1987.
- He completed two years of specialization in Corporate Finance at the Stern School of Business at New York University as a recipient of the "Donato Menichella" scholarship from Banca d'Italia.
- He began his career as a business consultant for Italian firms and multinationals in 1988, gaining international experience across industries including mechanics, consumer goods, financial institutions, and pharmaceuticals.
- In 1996, he founded a group of companies focused on technology and digital automation platforms, which he developed for 20 years.
- He is Director of the Leonardo Del Vecchio Foundation and of the IEO European Institute of Oncology.
- In 2025, he was awarded the honor of "Cavaliere del Lavoro" by the President of the Italian Republic.
- He was involved in the business combination between Essilor and Luxottica from January 2017, working closely with Paul du Saillant on integration and synergy plans.
- He was appointed CEO of EssilorLuxottica in December 2020 and Chairman and CEO on June 28, 2022.

The page also lists the full Board of Directors of EssilorLuxottica, including Paul du Saillant (Deputy CEO), and various independent and non-independent directors, as well as directors representing employees and the Valoptic Association.

PARIS, April 28 (Reuters) - The head of EssilorLuxottica [(ESLX.PA), opens new tab](https://www.reuters.com/markets/companies/ESLX.PA) expressed confidence a push into medical ‌technology would eventually drive a recovery in the market value of the world's largest eyewear group, after contributing to the sharp drop seen in recent months.

Speaking at the group's annual general meeting on ​Tuesday, EssilorLuxottica CEO Francesco Milleri listed other factors behind the share price fall ​of more than 40% from record highs hit in November: U.S. tariffs, the weakness ⁠of the dollar, spreading military conflicts and competition on smart glasses.

Finance chief Stefano Grassi quantified in ​300 million euros ($351 million) the impact from U.S. tariffs last year.

Milleri said investors had not ​fully understood EssilorLuxottica's expansion into the medtech sector, which he described as a necessary transformation.

"We were too big to remain ... (confined to) this small market," he said, referring to the group' s traditional spectacle frame and ​lens business.

"We are really pushing to go back to the (price) position that we deserve ... but, ​at the same time, it will take some time to achieve that", Milleri said.

The line chart shows the daily price evolution of the EssilorLuxottica stock since October.

## AUDIO SEGMENT SEEN AS ‌A ⁠GROWTH AREA

EssilorLuxottica's market value has shrunk to 86 billion euros from 150 billion in November, when it reached a record high [thanks to investor bets](https://www.reuters.com/business/shares-ray-ban-maker-essilorluxottica-soar-after-meta-ai-glasses-drive-revenue-2025-10-17/) on smartglasses which EssilorLuxottica develops in partnership with Meta Platforms.

Since then, however, growing competition in the segment has tempered investor ​enthusiasm.

Milleri said AI-powered glasses ​remained a key ⁠pillar for the group's strategy and played down concerns about rising competition.

"A few big players have made product announcements generating buzz, but we haven't ​seen any real competing products on the market so far," he said.

He ​pointed also ⁠to the [audio segment](https://www.reuters.com/business/healthcare-pharmaceuticals/essilorluxottica-considered-investing-amplifon-past-ceo-says-2026-04-28/) as a major growth area for EssilorLuxottica, with new products beyond Nuance Audio glasses, spectacles that incorporate hearing assistance for people with mild to moderate hearing loss.

Speaking ⁠to reporters ​on the sidelines of the meeting, Milleri said EssilorLuxottica ​had even weighed a possible investment in [Italian hearing](https://www.reuters.com/business/healthcare-pharmaceuticals/essilorluxottica-considered-investing-amplifon-past-ceo-says-2026-04-28/) aid maker Amplifon [(AMPF.MI), opens new tab](https://www.reuters.com/markets/companies/AMPF.MI), but had not pursued it.

On April 28, 2026, Reuters reported that EssilorLuxottica CEO Francesco Milleri expressed confidence at the group's annual general meeting in Paris that its push into medical technology (medtech) would eventually drive a recovery in its share price. The world's largest eyewear group saw its stock fall more than 40% from record highs hit in November 2025, attributed to U.S. tariffs, the weak dollar, spreading military conflicts, and growing smartglasses competition. The company's market value dropped to 86 billion euros from 150 billion euros at its November peak, which had been driven by investor bets on AI-powered smartglasses developed in partnership with Meta Platforms.

Finance chief Stefano Grassi quantified the impact from U.S. tariffs last year at 300 million euros ($351 million). Milleri argued that investors had not fully understood EssilorLuxottica's expansion into medtech, which he described as a necessary transformation: "We were too big to remain ... (confined to) this small market," referring to the traditional spectacle frame and lens business. He said the company is "really pushing to go back to the (price) position that we deserve ... but, at the same time, it will take some time to achieve that."

Regarding smartglasses competition, Milleri downplayed concerns, stating: "A few big players have made product announcements generating buzz, but we haven't seen any real competing products on the market so far." He highlighted the audio segment as a major growth area, with new products planned beyond the existing Nuance Audio glasses (spectacles with hearing assistance for mild to moderate hearing loss). Milleri also revealed that EssilorLuxottica had considered but not pursued a potential investment in Italian hearing aid maker Amplifon. The article was written by Elisa Anzolin and edited by Valentina Za and Mark Potter.

# A growing threat: Darren Woods on how policy is undermining energy

* Regulatory overreach is creating uncertainty and making long-term investments harder.
* Strong global partnerships help protect energy security and competitiveness.

Article

2 min read

 •  Feb. 11, 2026

## Navigate to:

## Darren Woods delivered a clear message

**DOHA, Qatar** – At [LNG 2026](https://lng2026.com/), Chairman and CEO Darren Woods delivered a clear message: reliable energy requires steady investment and practical policy.

Joined on stage by global energy leaders, Darren spoke about the essential role LNG will continue to play in meeting global energy demand. Many regions depend on this affordable, lower-emission fuel to support the growth of their economies. [Our long partnership with Qatar](/locations/qatar/qatar-newsroom/together-we-build-more-than-energy) is one example of how we support this need through scale and technology.

However, regulatory overreach like we’re seeing in Europe is creating uncertainty. These policies put a very high hurdle on continuing to invest and provide products in Europe. This leads to reduced supply, less stability, and higher costs for consumers.

The EU’s Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) is the leading example of policy that could have critical ramifications for future investments in the region. While the policy has been modified because of our advocacy, it still has extraterritorial requirements that mean, as Darren said, “if you want to do business in Europe, then you have to open your entire portfolio, your entire corporation, up to lawsuits out of Europe.”

A version of this scenario has emerged in Germany. An environmental group is using the country’s supply chain due-diligence law to challenge LNG imports, arguing that “fracked gas” violates environmental standards and should face regulatory consequences. If successful, this kind of legal pressure will likely push utility companies away from long-term contracts, risking future energy security.

To stay competitive, Europe needs to balance its net zero ambition with its practical need for affordable, reliable energy and energy products. Darren emphasized that what European policymakers were “advocating for was wholesale disruption and [to] throw out everything we've – as an industry – built over the last 140 years and try to replace it, almost instantaneously, which was never going to work.”

Future policies should support innovation in emissions reductions and encourage long-term investment in affordable energy supply. LNG plays a central role in that balance. It strengthens energy security while advancing lower-emission progress.

ExxonMobil remains committed to delivering reliable energy across the globe. To continue this work, supportive policy in the regions where we operate is essential. With the right policies in place, we can work to improve energy security and reduce emissions.

[Learn more here](/locations/european-region/eu-policy).

- Woods criticized European policymakers for advocating "wholesale disruption" and attempting to instantly replace 140 years of industry infrastructure, which he said "was never going to work."
- Woods called for policies that balance net-zero ambitions with practical needs for affordable, reliable energy, supporting innovation in emissions reductions and encouraging long-term investment.
- ExxonMobil remains committed to delivering reliable energy globally but requires supportive policy in the regions where it operates.

This is a CNBC "Squawk Box" interview with Exxon Mobil Chairman and CEO Darren Woods, discussing the company's Q1 earnings results and its response to the Middle East conflict, specifically the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The interview was posted on May 1, 2026, and the stock was up just over half a percent following better-than-expected quarterly results.

Key points from the interview:

1. **Earnings and Strategy**: ExxonMobil beat expectations in Q1. Woods emphasized that since 2018, the company has avoided predicting oil prices and instead focused on low-cost production growth based on its unique capabilities. He noted that production is needed worldwide to grow economies and improve lifestyles, regardless of market conditions.

2. **Production Growth**: Since 2018, ExxonMobil has more than doubled its U.S. production, growing at over 10% compounded annual growth rate. The company was the only U.S. company to expand refining production in 2023, with a 200,000 barrels-per-day improvement that has already paid for itself. The company also started its LNG plant on the Gulf Coast, which increases U.S. LNG exports by about 5%.

3. **Middle East Conflict Impact**: Approximately 20% of ExxonMobil's total production is in the Middle East, with about 15% of production impacted by the Strait of Hormuz closure (the strait closure itself being the challenge, not damage to facilities). Only 3% of the company's facilities were impacted. The company redeployed about 13 million barrels to get oil to the markets that need it most.

4. **Derivatives and Timing**: Because of the large volume of barrel movements, ExxonMobil's trading organization put hedges in place to lock in profits. The physical barrels remain in inventory until delivery, creating deferred profit that was highlighted in the earnings release to explain a loss booked in the current quarter that will be made up in a future quarter.

5. **Oil Price Outlook**: Woods called the supply disruption "unprecedented." He estimated that once the Strait of Hormuz reopens, it will take 1-2 months for flow to reestablish, plus about a month of transit time to get barrels from the Persian Gulf to demand destinations. So far, the impact has been mitigated by oil in transit when the strait closed, Strategic Petroleum Reserve releases, and commercial inventory draws — but these mitigating factors will run out if the strait remains closed, and prices will eventually respond to the supply disruption.
args.key_excerpts: "We never try to predict prices. We recognize one, that the markets are volatile and certain. Two, that the products that we produce, the energy we produce, is needed all around the world to continue to grow economies and to improve people's lifestyles." - Darren Woods

**Darren Wayne Woods** (born December 16, 1965)[[1]](#cite_note-1) is an American businessman who has been the CEO and chairman of [ExxonMobil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ExxonMobil "ExxonMobil") since January 2017.[[2]](#cite_note-corp-2)

## Early life

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Darren_Woods&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Woods was born in [Wichita, Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wichita,_Kansas "Wichita, Kansas"). Due to his father's work as a military supplier, he spent much of his youth living near various U.S. military bases around the world.[[3]](#cite_note-3) He earned a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from [Texas A&M University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_A&M_University "Texas A&M University"), followed by an MBA from [Northwestern University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwestern_University "Northwestern University")'s [Kellogg School of Management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kellogg_School_of_Management "Kellogg School of Management").[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)

## Career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Darren_Woods&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### ExxonMobil

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Darren_Woods&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: ExxonMobil")]

Woods joined Exxon in 1992. He had worked for Exxon for 24 years prior to being promoted to CEO following [Rex Tillerson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rex_Tillerson "Rex Tillerson")'s nomination by President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") to be the next [United States Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State").[[2]](#cite_note-corp-2)[[6]](#cite_note-6) While his predecessor was involved in deal making and exploration, Woods is a veteran of the [refining](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oil_refinery "Oil refinery") side of the oil business.[[7]](#cite_note-cbs-7) Prior to becoming CEO, Woods ran the refining and chemical divisions of the company, which delivered the majority of ExxonMobil's $7.8 billion net income in 2016.[[8]](#cite_note-forbes-8)

At an investor meeting in New York in 2017, Woods outlined his growth plan including drilling in the [Permian Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permian_Basin_(North_America) "Permian Basin (North America)") of Texas and New Mexico and the [Bakken shale formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bakken_shale_formation "Bakken shale formation") in North Dakota. He also spoke briefly about the company's operations in Russia, expressing an optimistic outlook regarding Exxon's [Sakhalin project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sakhalin-I "Sakhalin-I") on Russia's eastern coast.[[7]](#cite_note-cbs-7)

Woods has said that the combination of [horizontal drilling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horizontal_drilling "Horizontal drilling") and [hydraulic fracturing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydraulic_fracturing "Hydraulic fracturing") has "shattered the [Peak Oil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_Oil "Peak Oil") myth".[[8]](#cite_note-forbes-8) Woods has publicly endorsed the [Paris Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Agreement "Paris Agreement"). The accord commits nations to cutting greenhouse gas emissions.[[9]](#cite_note-9) In May 2017, Woods wrote a personal letter to President Trump to urge that the U.S. remain a party to the agreement and not [withdraw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_withdrawal_from_the_Paris_Agreement "United States withdrawal from the Paris Agreement"). He says that by remaining a party to the accords the U.S. will have a seat at the table to "ensure a level playing field" and support "the most cost-effective greenhouse gas reduction options".[[10]](#cite_note-10)

On October 5, 2020, [Bloomberg News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomberg_News "Bloomberg News") reported that Exxon was set to increase its annual carbon emissions by about 17%, or about as much as the annual output of [Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greece "Greece"). The emissions expansion would be built off an investment plan reportedly signed off by Woods. Exxon said its internal projections are "a preliminary, internal assessment of estimated cumulative emission growth through 2025 and did not include the [additional] mitigation and abatement measures that would have been evaluated in the planning process. Furthermore, the projections identified in the leaked documents have significantly changed, a fact that was not fully explained or prominently featured in the article."[[11]](#cite_note-11)

In 2022, Woods was named one of the US' top "climate villains" by *[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Guardian "The Guardian")* after "Exxon lobbyists were captured on video revealing the company's efforts to obstruct climate legislation in Congress."[[12]](#cite_note-12)

Woods claimed in an interview with [CNBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNBC "CNBC") journalist [David Faber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Faber_(journalist) "David Faber (journalist)") in June 2022 that part of ExxonMobil's long-term strategy to remain a profitable company while reducing greenhouse gas emissions and [plastic pollution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plastic_pollution "Plastic pollution") was to invest in [carbon capture and storage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_capture_and_storage "Carbon capture and storage") technology with a network hub in [Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston "Houston") and to remain a [plastics producer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plastics_industry "Plastics industry") while making changes to [waste management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waste_management "Waste management").[[13]](#cite_note-13)[[14]](#cite_note-14) Woods also called for a higher [carbon price](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_price "Carbon price").[[15]](#cite_note-15) In April 2024, Woods stated on the company quarterly [earnings call](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earnings_call "Earnings call") that while the company was continuing to develop [direct air capture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_air_capture "Direct air capture") (DAC) technology, DAC was currently unaffordable at $600 to $1,000 per ton of [carbon dioxide removal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_dioxide_removal "Carbon dioxide removal") and needed to be brought down to $100 per ton to be globally scalable.[[16]](#cite_note-16)

On December 8, 2023, Woods attended the Chemical Marketing & Economics gala in New York City, to be honored with a "STEM leadership award" for "harnessing the transformative power of chemistry to advance humanity".[[17]](#cite_note-17) Because of his role in increasing oil and gas consumption, a group of climate activists disrupted and brought an end to the gala. They carried a banner that notably read "Eat shit Darren".[[18]](#cite_note-18)

In 2021, *[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Guardian "The Guardian")* reported that Woods' salary exceeded $20,000,000 per year.[[19]](#cite_note-19) In 2023, Woods's total compensation from ExxonMobil was $31 million, representing a CEO-to-median worker [pay ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wage_ratio "Wage ratio") of 199-to-1.[[20]](#cite_note-20) In 2024, his compensation rose to $44.1 million, with a pay ratio of 231-to-1.[[21]](#cite_note-21)

In November 2024, Woods stated in an interview that the [second Trump administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_presidency_of_Donald_Trump "Second presidency of Donald Trump") should not withdraw from the Paris Agreement and that ExxonMobil company investments in CCS and DAC would change if tax credits established under the [Inflation Reduction Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inflation_Reduction_Act "Inflation Reduction Act") are repealed or reduced.[[22]](#cite_note-22)[[23]](#cite_note-23)

He is a member of [The Business Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Business_Council "The Business Council").[[24]](#cite_note-24)

#### Alleged lying to Congress

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Darren_Woods&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Alleged lying to Congress")]

In 2021, Woods denied that Exxon had covered up its own research about [Big Oil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Oil "Big Oil")'s contribution to the climate crisis. The chair of the Congressional committee taking Woods' testimony likened Woods' denial to the decades' long lies by the American [tobacco industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tobacco_industry "Tobacco industry") denying that [nicotine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicotine "Nicotine") is addictive.[[25]](#cite_note-:0-25) Woods also declined to make a pledge to stop lobbying against [climate initiatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change_mitigation "Climate change mitigation").[[25]](#cite_note-:0-25)

Darren Wayne Woods (born December 16, 1965, in Wichita, Kansas) is an American businessman who has served as CEO and chairman of ExxonMobil since January 2017, succeeding Rex Tillerson. He is the 23rd President (assumed office January 1, 2016) and 16th Chairman (assumed office January 1, 2017) of ExxonMobil.

EDUCATION AND EARLY LIFE: Woods earned a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from Texas A&M University and an MBA from Northwestern University's Kellogg School of Management. Due to his father's work as a military supplier, he spent much of his youth living near U.S. military bases worldwide.

CAREER AT EXXONMOBIL: Woods joined Exxon in 1992 and worked there for 24 years before being promoted to CEO following Tillerson's nomination by President Donald Trump to be Secretary of State. He is a veteran of the refining side of the oil business (unlike his deal-making predecessor) and previously ran the company's refining and chemical divisions, which delivered the majority of ExxonMobil's $7.8 billion net income in 2016.

KEY POLICY POSITIONS AND EVENTS:
- At a 2017 investor meeting, he outlined growth plans for drilling in the Permian Basin (Texas/New Mexico) and the Bakken shale formation (North Dakota), and expressed optimism about Exxon's Sakhalin project in Russia.
- He has said horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing have "shattered the Peak Oil myth."
- He publicly endorsed the Paris Agreement and wrote a personal letter to President Trump in May 2017 urging the U.S. to remain a party to the accord.
- In October 2020, Bloomberg News reported Exxon was set to increase annual carbon emissions by ~17% (about as much as Greece's annual output) based on an investment plan reportedly signed off by Woods; Exxon disputed the characterization of leaked documents.
- In 2022, The Guardian named Woods one of America's top "climate villains" after Exxon lobbyists were captured on video revealing efforts to obstruct climate legislation in Congress.
- In June 2022, Woods told CNBC that Exxon's strategy included investing in carbon capture and storage (CCS) technology with a Houston hub and remaining a plastics producer while changing waste management; he also called for a higher carbon price.
- In April 2024, he stated that direct air capture (DAC) technology was currently unaffordable at $600-$1,000 per ton of CO2 removal and needed to be brought down to $100 per ton to be globally scalable.
- In November 2024, he stated the second Trump administration should not withdraw from the Paris Agreement and that Exxon's CCS and DAC investments would change if Inflation Reduction Act tax credits are repealed.
- In December 2023, a gala honoring him with a "STEM leadership award" was disrupted by climate activists carrying a banner reading "Eat shit Darren."

COMPENSATION: His salary exceeded $20 million/year as of 2021. In 2023, total compensation was $31 million (199-to-1 CEO-to-median-worker pay ratio); in 2024, it rose to $44.1 million (231-to-1 ratio).

ALLEGED LYING TO CONGRESS: In 2021, Woods denied that Exxon covered up its own research about Big Oil's contribution to the climate crisis. The Congressional committee chair likened this denial to the tobacco industry's decades-long lies about nicotine addiction. Woods also declined to pledge to stop lobbying against climate initiatives.

# Darren W. Woods

Chairman and CEO, ExxonMobil Corporation

Image

![Darren W. Woods](https://csis-website-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/styles/224_x_224/s3/2022-09/5Woods.jpg?VersionId=9lXRZeCzfML.2ndMnjP7iCtpjt46D97B&itok=czxZf1aK)

Darren Woods is a graduate of Texas A&M University, where he earned a Bachelor of Science degree in electrical engineering. He also holds a Master of Business Administration degree from Northwestern's Kellogg School of Management in Evanston, Illinois. Mr. Woods joined Exxon Company International in 1992 as a planning analyst in Florham Park, New Jersey. He progressed through a number of domestic and international assignments for Exxon Company International, ExxonMobil Chemical Company and ExxonMobil Refining and Supply Company. In 2005, Mr. Woods was appointed vice president of ExxonMobil Chemical Company in Houston, Texas, where he managed global specialty-chemical businesses. In 2008, he was named ExxonMobil Refining and Supply Company’s director of refining for Europe, Africa and the Middle East, and was based in Brussels. In 2010, he was appointed vice president of supply and transportation, based in Fairfax, Virginia. Mr. Woods was appointed president of ExxonMobil Refining and Supply Company and vice president of Exxon Mobil Corporation in 2012. In 2014, Mr. Woods was elected senior vice president of Exxon Mobil Corporation. Effective January 1, 2016, Mr. Woods was elected president of Exxon Mobil Corporation and a member of the board of directors. The ExxonMobil Board of Directors elected Mr. Woods as Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, effective January 1, 2017. Mr. Woods is currently the Chairman of the American Petroleum Institute and a member of its executive committee. He is also a member of the National Petroleum Council, the Business Roundtable, the Business Council and the Texas A&M University Engineering Advisory Council.

# CEO Pay: The $25 Million Plus Pay Club (2026)

Boardroom Alpha’s 2026 ranking of every U.S. public-company CEO paid $25M+ in fiscal 2025 — 207 in all, led by Welltower Inc’s $821.1M package, which drew just 19% Say-on-Pay support. Sortable table, pay-vs-performance, and board grades.

In May 2026, **Welltower Inc (WELL)** handed Shankh Mitra the largest pay package on this list — **$821.1M** — after a year in which the stock rose 40%. Shareholders rejected it anyway: only **19%** backed the company’s Say-on-Pay vote, among the most lopsided repudiations of a sitting CEO’s pay on record.

Months earlier, the verdict had run the other way on a far larger number. At **Tesla Inc (TSLA)**’s November 2025 meeting, shareholders approved a new award for Elon Musk worth as much as **$878 billion** — roughly $1 trillion if every milestone is met, the largest grant in corporate history — with about **75%** support. Same season, opposite result: investors spurned the biggest package on this ranking and blessed one in a different universe of size.

That split is the year’s real lesson, and it is not about size. The fiscal-2025 club reached **207** U.S. public-company CEOs paid $25 million or more, up from 153, at a **$33.3M** median, with 14 one-time mega-grants stacked at the top. Investors pushed 27 of those packages below 70% support and failed 8 outright. What the revolts share is neither a dollar figure nor a stock chart — it is surprise.

## What Shareholders Actually Punish

The instinct is to read these revolts as a backlash against big pay. The data says otherwise. The largest grants of the cycle sailed through: Tesla’s holders approved Musk’s award with about 75% support, Opendoor Technologies Inc (OPEN) cleared Kaz Nejatian’s $741.1M with 97%, and Rivian Automotive Inc (RIVN) backed Robert Scaringe’s $402.6M with 92%. Size, plainly, is not the trigger.

Neither is performance. Seven of the eight packages that failed outright belonged to CEOs whose stock *rose* over the year — Welltower (+40%), Snowflake (+16%), Thermo Fisher (+21%), Warner Bros. Discovery (+183%), Element Solutions (+92%), Palo Alto Networks (+38%) and IQVIA (+29%). Meanwhile Comcast Corp (CMCSA) fell 20% on the year and still drew 90% support; underperformance, on its own, did not provoke a revolt.

What the rejections share is surprise. They cluster on first-time or unexpected mega-grants at companies whose shareholder base wasn’t conditioned for them — a healthcare REIT suddenly writing a nine-figure check, a software firm front-loading a multi-year award. Musk’s package, however enormous, was negotiated in the open and tied to hard milestones a base of holders had pre-committed to. The line shareholders draw is about process and expectation, not the number at the end.

## The Quiet Exits

22 of the 207 highest-paid CEOs (10.6%) have already left the job.

One in ten of the highest-paid is already gone. Of the 207 CEOs ranked here, **22 — 10.6%** no longer run the company as of publication (marked † throughout). The turnover reads like ordinary succession and dealmaking, not a shareholder purge: Walmart’s Doug McMillon handed off to John Furner, Coca-Cola’s James Quincey to Henrique Braun, and Nike’s John Donahoe to Elliott Hill, while Exact Sciences’ Kevin Conroy left when Abbott acquired the company. Just 1 of the 22 had drawn a Say-on-Pay revolt — below the rate for the club as a whole — so for this cohort the exit has had little to do with the pay backlash. It is a turnover rate worth watching: more than a tenth of the best-paid seats changed hands inside a single year.

args.summary:
Boardroom Alpha's 2026 ranking of U.S. public-company CEOs paid $25M+ in fiscal 2025 identifies 207 CEOs (up from 153 in FY2024), with a median package of $33.3M and average of $54.6M. The list is led by Welltower Inc's Shankh Mitra at $821.1M (which drew only 19% Say-on-Pay support despite a +40% stock rise), followed by Opendoor Technologies' Kaz Nejatian at $741.1M (97% support, +638% TSR), and Rivian's Robert Scaringe at $402.6M (92% support).

Key findings: (1) Shareholder revolts correlate with surprise/process, not size or performance — 27 packages drew under 70% Say-on-Pay support, and 8 failed outright (<50%); largest grants sailed through (Tesla's Musk award ~$878B with 75% support). (2) Fourteen one-time mega-grants (near-all-equity, booked in a single year) distort the picture. (3) 68 recurring-pay CEOs cleared $25M while their stock fell over the year; 30 were underwater over 3 years too; 47% of red-zone names carry board grades of C or worse. (4) 22 of the 207 highest-paid CEOs (10.6%) have already left their jobs. (5) Big pay tracks big companies — Technology (50 CEOs, $2.51B) and Financial Services (49 CEOs, $2.38B) hold the most; Real Estate's outsized block is almost entirely two mega-grants.

The deepest Say-on-Pay rejections include Welltower (18.9%), IQVIA (24.8%), Snowflake (30.2%), Thermo Fisher (31.8%), Beyond Meat (32.1%), Warner Bros. Discovery (40.5%), Element Solutions (41.4%), and Palo Alto Networks (46.6%). Milder dissents (55-69%) include Pfizer, UnitedHealth, Citigroup, Wells Fargo, and BlackRock.

The full sortable table lists all 207 CEOs with pay, YoY change, 1-year TSR, board rating, and Say-on-Pay support. Notable names: Elon Musk (Tesla, ~$878B award approved Nov 2025), Satya Nadella (Microsoft, $96.5M), Tim Cook (Apple, $74.3M), Jensen Huang (Nvidia, $49.9M), Jane Fraser (Citigroup, $95.8M), David Solomon (Goldman Sachs, $118.1M), and Stephen Schwarzman (Blackstone, $125.6M). Data is as of May 29, 2026.
args.key_excerpts: "In May 2026, Welltower Inc (WELL) handed Shankh Mitra the largest pay package on this list — $821.1M — after a year in which the stock rose 40%. Shareholders rejected it anyway: only 19% backed the company's Say-on-Pay vote, among the most lopsided repudiations of a sitting CEO's pay on record."

# Liz Claman

Liz Claman joined FOX Business Network (FBN) as an anchor in October 2007. She anchors *The Claman Countdown* (weekdays 3-4 PM ET). Claman was recently inducted into the Cable Hall of Fame.

Her debut on FBN included an exclusive interview with Berkshire Hathaway CEO and legendary investor Warren Buffett. Throughout her tenure with the network, Claman has conducted exclusive interviews with nearly every U.S. Treasury Secretary from John Snow to Paul O’Neill, Larry Summers, Timothy Geithner, Jack Lew and Steven Mnuchin.

Claman has also talked business with a roster of some of the biggest corporate leaders in the world, including Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, NVIDIA founder & CEO Jensen Huang, Microsoft’s Bill Gates, Apple’s Tim Cook, BlackRock’s Larry Fink, JP Morgan’s Jamie Dimon, Palantir’s Alex Karp, AirBNB’s Brian Chesky, Chevron’s Mike Wirth, General Motors’ Mary Barra, Netflix's co-CEO Ted Sarandos, AT&T’s John Stankey, Verizon’s Hans Vestberg, Adobe’s Shantanu Narayen, Qualcomm’s Cristiano Amon, Pfizer’s Albert Bourla, billionaire investor John Paulson, Former U.S. Ambassador to the United Kingdom and NY Jets owner Woody Johnson, Omega Advisors Chairman and CEO Leon Cooperman and billionaire entrepreneur Frank McCourt, Jr. to name just a few.

She has also interviewed world leaders, including Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, British Prime Ministers Tony Blair and Boris Johnson, and former Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko.

Additionally, Claman has reported from the Berkshire Hathaway Annual Shareholders Meeting in Omaha for more than a decade, where she has interviewed Buffett and his top corporate leaders, shareholders and investors in attendance. She has also covered the Consumer Electronics Show for close to two decades, where she has interviewed tech industry leaders including Delta CEO Ed Bastian, Nasdaq CEO Adena Friedman, IAC Chairperson Barry Diller, Arm CEO Rene Haas, billionaire Luminar founder and CEO Austin Russell, among others.

She also frequently interviews celebrities and athletes about their business ventures.  Some former guests include pro golfer Phil Mickelson, Boxing Legend Floyd Mayweather, Baseball Hall of Famer Derek Jeter, NHL Commissioner Gary Bettman, MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred, Minnesota Vikings co-owner Mark Wilf, New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft, Atlanta Falcons owner Arthur Blank, Cake Boss Buddy Valastro, fashion designer Rebecca Minkoff, singer-songwriter will.i.am as well as social media influencers Logan Paul, Costco Guys and The Rizzler.

Prior to joining FBN, Claman served as an anchor at CNBC, anchoring programs including Morning Call, Wake Up Call, Market Watch, and Today’s Business. During her time there, Claman landed the first ever one-hour live interview with Buffett.

Before CNBC, Claman served as an anchor and reporter for Boston’s WHDH-TV (NBC). She was also a contributing correspondent for NBC’s syndicated daytime program RealLife. Prior to that, she anchored a two-hour daily talk show, *The Morning Exchange*for WEWS-TV (ABC) in Cleveland, for which she won an Emmy Award.

A graduate of the University of California, Berkeley, and the Sorbonne in Paris, Claman began her on-air career at WSYX-TV (ABC) in Columbus, OH as a reporter and later a weekend anchor. Earlier, she was a news associate for KCBS-TV (CBS) in Los Angeles, where she was the youngest person in the station’s history to win a local Emmy Award for Best Spot News Producer.

Claman is a member of the Board of Directors of the American Theatre Wing and is a Tony Award voter. She is also an active fundraiser for Building Homes for Heroes, an organization that builds mortgage-free homes for severely wounded veterans and has completed seven triathlons and one New York City marathon.

This is a Fox Business biography page for Liz Claman, a prominent anchor who joined FOX Business Network (FBN) in October 2007. She anchors *The Claman Countdown*, airing weekdays from 3-4 PM ET, and was recently inducted into the Cable Hall of Fame.

Her notable career highlights include:
- Her debut on FBN featured an exclusive interview with Berkshire Hathaway CEO Warren Buffett, and she landed the first ever one-hour live interview with Buffett during her time at CNBC.
- She has interviewed nearly every U.S. Treasury Secretary from John Snow through Steven Mnuchin.
- She has conducted exclusive interviews with major corporate leaders including Elon Musk (Tesla/SpaceX), Jensen Huang (NVIDIA), Bill Gates (Microsoft), Tim Cook (Apple), Larry Fink (BlackRock), Jamie Dimon (JP Morgan), Alex Karp (Palantir), and Brian Chesky (Airbnb), among many others.
- She has interviewed world leaders including Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu, British PMs Tony Blair and Boris Johnson, and former Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko.
- She has reported from the Berkshire Hathaway Annual Shareholders Meeting in Omaha for over a decade and covered the Consumer Electronics Show for nearly two decades.
- She frequently interviews celebrities and athletes about their business ventures, including Phil Mickelson, Floyd Mayweather, Derek Jeter, and others.

Prior to FBN, Claman worked at CNBC anchoring programs including Morning Call, Wake Up Call, Market Watch, and Today's Business. Earlier in her career, she anchored at WHDH-TV (NBC) in Boston, won an Emmy for her work at WEWS-TV (ABC) in Cleveland on *The Morning Exchange*, and began her career at WSYX-TV (ABC) in Columbus, OH. She was the youngest person in KCBS-TV (CBS) history in Los Angeles to win a local Emmy for Best Spot News Producer.

Claman graduated from the University of California, Berkeley, and the Sorbonne in Paris. She serves on the Board of Directors of the American Theatre Wing, is a Tony Award voter, raises funds for Building Homes for Heroes (which builds mortgage-free homes for wounded veterans), and has completed seven triathlons and one New York City marathon.

The page also includes a list of recent video segments from The Claman Countdown, covering topics such as Lumentum shares surging 600% amid AI demand, rising U.S. debt approaching $40 trillion, Amazon/AWS growth, small-cap stocks and the Russell 2000, and AI infrastructure developments.

By tethering ExxonMobil’s future to fickle policy whims instead of the durable competitive advantage it has enjoyed for decades, Mr. Woods has violated the first principle of fiduciary duty: safeguarding shareholder capital from foreseeable risk. The board’s refusal to separate the chair and CEO roles, or to erase climate-linked pay incentives, further entrenches this misalignment. Shareholders therefore face a stark choice in 2025: Endorse leadership that bets Company equity on Washington, D.C.’s subsidy pipeline, or signal – through a decisive “**Against**” vote – that ExxonMobil must return to the strategic discipline that once made it the industry benchmark. NLPC recommends the latter course.

**NLPC’s 2024 Campaign – and Why It Matters in 2025**

NLPC has engaged ExxonMobil for two consecutive proxy seasons, warning that management’s subsidy-driven “energy-transition” agenda threatens long-term shareholder value. At the 2024 annual meeting,[2](#_ftnf2) NLPC asked the Compensation Committee to stop awarding bonuses tied to greenhouse-gas targets that encourage capital diversion into speculative carbon-capture and storage (“CCS”) projects, when that investment could be steered into the Company’s more stable, proven, high-return hydrocarbon business. We stressed that CCS returns depend almost entirely on Inflation Reduction Act tax credits that could vanish with a change in U.S. political leadership. Management opposed our proposal, and has since doubled down on carbon dioxide recovery schemes, a byproduct of scientifically flimsy climate alarmism.[3](#_ftnf3)

Climate Change Conference.[6](#_ftnf6)  We believe Mr. Woods’s comments were a breach of fiduciary duty. According to the *New York Times:[7](#_ftnf7)*

Darren Woods, the chief executive of ExxonMobil, cautioned President-elect Donald J. Trump on Tuesday against withdrawing from the Paris agreement to curb climate-warming emissions, saying Mr. Trump risked leaving a void at the negotiating table.

President Trump withdrew the U.S. from the Paris Agreement during his first term. President Joe Biden reentered the agreement not long after taking office in 2021.[8](#_ftnf8) Mr. Woods told the *Wall Street Journal*: “I don’t think the stops and starts are the right thing for businesses. It is extremely inefficient. It creates a lot of uncertainty.”[9](#_ftnf9)

Further, Mr. Woods also defended the Inflation Reduction Act (“IRA”), signed into law by President Biden,[10](#_ftnf10) because ExxonMobil has become reliant on government subsidies and special tax treatment for its carbon capture initiatives:[11](#_ftnf11)

Woods told CNBC on Tuesday that Exxon’s investments in technologies to lower emissions depend on federal tax credits that were established or expanded under the IRA. He warned that the company’s investments in these technologies would change if the incentives are weakened or repealed.

Shareholders must ask: What kind of leadership *is this* at ExxonMobil?

**Conclusion**

These facts leave shareholders only one remaining remedy in 2025: to vote against Mr. Woods for the board of directors. Doing so would send a message to the Board of Directors that shareholders demand they restore strategic discipline and refocus the company on the hydrocarbon mastery that built its franchise.

By endorsing the IRA and other subsidy-driven gimmicks and schemes, Mr. Woods has subjected the Company to volatile political dynamics and regulatory risks that could diminish its profitability if government policies are scaled back or repealed. This approach undermines ExxonMobil’s traditional strengths in the energy sector, relying on the goodwill of policymakers rather than market-driven demand for hydrocarbon energy.

ExxonMobil’s legacy and competitive advantage have been built on the exploration, extraction, and refinement of hydrocarbons[29](#_ftnf29) – assets essential to the global economy. Pivoting to ventures that are unprofitable without government subsidies and mandates, under the guise of climate stewardship, weakens the Company’s position within the energy market, particularly as other oil and gas competitors capitalize on unmet global demand. This path also represents a breach of Mr. Woods’s fiduciary duty to maximize shareholder value and protect the company’s long-term stability.

Further, evidence is mounting that CCS presents risks related to property rights, eminent domain, energy cost increases, and safety.[30](#_ftnf30)

Meanwhile, Exxon’s traditional franchise – long-life, low-cost barrels in the Permian and Guyana – requires disciplined capital to sustain advantaged break-evens. Every dollar diverted to speculative decarbonization erodes that moat and hands market share to competitors willing to keep drilling.

Nor does Mr. Woods’s political calculus hedge downside. If U.S. policy swings away from Paris-style commitments, subsidy cash flows evaporate and carbon-capture assets will be stranded. Shareholders should not have to subsidize political ideology – a direct violation of fiduciary standards governing duty of loyalty and care.

Shareholders therefore face a simple choice: endorse leadership that bets the company’s future on fickle politics, or insist on a board chair who restores market discipline, re-focuses on high-return hydrocarbons, and evaluates lower-carbon ventures only when they generate acceptable risk-adjusted returns without government transfer payments. Voting against Mr. Woods is the most immediate, proportionate step available to realign ExxonMobil with the durable principles that have made it an industry benchmark.

args.summary:
This is a Notice of Exempt Solicitation (SEC Rule 14a-103) filed by the National Legal and Policy Center (NLPC), a nonprofit based in Falls Church, VA, urging Exxon Mobil Corporation shareholders to vote AGAINST the re-election of CEO Darren W. Woods (Nominee No. 12) to the Board of Directors on the 2025 proxy ballot (annual meeting held May 28, 2025).

Key arguments by NLPC:

1. **Subsidy-Dependent Climate Ventures**: NLPC argues that under Woods's leadership, ExxonMobil has shifted away from its historically profitable hydrocarbon strategy toward politically contingent, subsidy-driven climate projects (carbon capture and storage/CCS, hydrogen, biofuels, lithium) that depend on Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) federal tax credits. These credits could be eliminated with a change in political leadership, stranding billions in capital and exposing investors to write-downs.

2. **COP29/Political Commentary**: On November 14, 2024, NLPC wrote to ExxonMobil's board calling for Woods's resignation after he publicly urged then-President-elect Trump not to withdraw from the Paris Climate Agreement. Woods told the Wall Street Journal: "I don't think the stops and starts are the right thing for businesses. It is extremely inefficient. It creates a lot of uncertainty." Woods also defended the IRA because Exxon's lower-carbon investments depend on its tax credits, warning investments "would change if the incentives are weakened or repealed." NLPC deemed these comments a breach of fiduciary duty.

3. **Pro-Carbon Regulation Stance**: While competitors like Chevron and Shell praised the new Trump administration's direction, Woods continued advocating for global CO2 emissions regulations, urging "product-level carbon-intensity standards." Exxon plans to invest up to $30 billion into hydrogen, carbon capture, biofuels, and lithium production through 2030, investments NLPC argues remain unprofitable even with subsidies.

4. **Engine No. 1 Board Insurgency**: NLPC asserts Woods was influenced by the 2021 board insurgency of three Engine No. 1-nominated directors, coinciding with significant CCS investments. NLPC cites a U.S. House Judiciary Committee finding of a "climate cartel" of activist investors and notes Engine No. 1 has since partnered with Chevron on natural gas power plants for data centers.

5. **Compensation Concerns**: Woods's pay package rose 19.3% to $44.1 million in 2024, which NLPC suggests may be linked to his climate agenda.

6. **Other Director Concerns**: NLPC also criticizes the appointment of former Boeing Chairman Larry Kellner to the board's safety committee (2023) and the elevation of Dan Ammann to President of ExxonMobil Upstream Company (late 2024), who was previously fired by General Motors after running its autonomous driving division poorly.

7. **Governance Issues**: Woods holds both CEO and Chair titles, concentrating power and limiting board oversight. NLPC warns of risks from potential subsidy clawbacks, greenwashing claims, and CCS risks related to property rights, eminent domain, energy cost increases, and safety.

NLPC concludes that voting against Woods would signal shareholders demand a return to strategic discipline focused on high-return hydrocarbons (Permian and Guyana long-life, low-cost barrels) and that market-driven demand, not government subsidies, should guide ExxonMobil's capital allocation.
args.key_excerpts: "By tethering ExxonMobil's future to fickle policy whims instead of the durable competitive advantage it has enjoyed for decades, Mr. Woods has violated the first principle of fiduciary duty: safeguarding shareholder capital from foreseeable risk."

**Henry Lawrence "Larry" Culp, Jr.** (born March 1963) is an American business executive. He is chairman and CEO of [GE Aerospace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GE_Aerospace "GE Aerospace").[[1]](#cite_note-Logan-1)[[2]](#cite_note-:0-2) He is the first outsider to run GE in the company's 126-year history.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

Prior to joining GE, Culp worked at Pall Corporation and [Danaher Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danaher_Corporation "Danaher Corporation") in Washington, D.C. He joined the Danaher Corporation in 1990 and was CEO from 2001 through 2014. Culp joined the GE board of directors in April 2018.[[1]](#cite_note-Logan-1)

## Early life and education

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Larry_Culp&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Culp was born and raised in the Washington, D.C. area, the son of a small welding company owner. He earned a bachelor's degree from [Washington College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_College "Washington College"), and an MBA from [Harvard Business School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Business_School "Harvard Business School").[[1]](#cite_note-Logan-1)

## Career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Larry_Culp&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Culp joined Danaher in 1990 via the subsidiary [Veeder-Root](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilbarco_Veeder-Root "Gilbarco Veeder-Root"), and became President of that company 1993. He was appointed a group executive and corporate officer in 1995, with responsibility for [Danaher’s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danaher_Corporation "Danaher Corporation") Environmental and Electronic Test and Measurement platforms while also being President of [Fluke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluke_Corporation "Fluke Corporation") and Fluke Networks. He was named an Executive Vice President in 1999, Chief Operating Officer in 2001, and President as well as CEO in 2001. Previously, Culp was a senior lecturer at Harvard Business School, where he focused on leadership, strategy and general management in the MBA and executive education programs.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

Culp is also a senior advisor at [Bain Capital Private Equity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bain_Capital "Bain Capital") and a non-executive director of [T. Rowe Price](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._Rowe_Price "T. Rowe Price").[[5]](#cite_note-5)

Culp's pay package of up to $21 million a year for four years as chairman and CEO of [General Electric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Electric "General Electric") has attracted attention, especially the element tied to any stock price increase, with about $47 million for a 50% rise and perhaps $300 million for a 150% increase.[[6]](#cite_note-CNBC-6) In 2020, Culp was offered a contract-extension of two years by the board of General Electric that would last until August 2024.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

In April 2021, the [Financial Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_Times "Financial Times") reported that Culp faced push back from two of the largest shareholder advisers on his pay package, which includes a bonus of $47 million.[[8]](#cite_note-8) In June 2022, Culp extended his role as CEO of [GE Aviation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GE_Aviation "GE Aviation"), in addition to GE.[[2]](#cite_note-:0-2) Following [GE HealthCare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GE_HealthCare "GE HealthCare")'s spin-off from GE in January 2023, Culp was appointed as its non-executive chairman.[[9]](#cite_note-9) Culp's total compensation for 2024 was $87.4 million.[[10]](#cite_note-10)

## Personal life

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Larry_Culp&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Culp is married, with three children,[[11]](#cite_note-Financial_Times-11) and lives in the Boston area.[[1]](#cite_note-Logan-1)

# H. Lawrence 'Larry' Culp

## Chairman and CEO

GE Aerospace

H. Lawrence (Larry) Culp, Jr., is the Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of GE and Chief Executive Officer of GE Aerospace. Larry is GE’s twelfth CEO and eleventh Chairman. He joined the [GE Board of Directors](https://www.ge.com/investor-relations/governance) in April 2018 and was appointed CEO of GE in October 2018. In June 2022, he was appointed CEO of GE Aerospace. As CEO, Larry has led GE’s transformation to become a more focused, simpler, and stronger high-tech industrial company.

Under his leadership, GE’s total gross debt reduction will be more than $90 billion through 2022. He has championed lean, bringing a focus on customer value, driving improvements in safety, quality, delivery, and cost, and running the company closer to the customer by creating nearly thirty P&Ls to increase operational visibility. Larry has also led the transformation of GE’s portfolio, including the sales of GE Capital Aviation Services (GECAS), Lighting, BioPharma, and the completion of the spin of GE Transportation along with its subsequent merger with Wabtec.

In November 2021, GE announced its plan to form three industry-leading, global public companies focused on the high-growth sectors of aviation, healthcare and energy. Larry will serve as non-executive chairman of the GE healthcare company upon its expected spin-off in early 2023. He will continue to serve as chairman and CEO of GE and CEO of GE Aerospace until the spin-off of the combined GE Renewable Energy and Power businesses, at which point, he will lead the GE aviation-focused company going forward.

Prior to joining GE, Larry served as the President and CEO of Danaher Corporation from 2000 to 2014, and during his tenure the company increased both its revenues and its market capitalization five-fold. Investors and analysts consistently ranked him as one of the top CEOs in annual Institutional Investor surveys, and Harvard Business Review named Larry one of the Top 50 CEOs in the world.

Larry joined Danaher in 1990 at Veeder-Root, becoming President in 1993. He was appointed Group Executive and Corporate Officer in 1995, with responsibility for Danaher’s Environmental and Electronic Test and Measurement platforms while also serving as President of Fluke and Fluke Networks. He was named Executive Vice President in 1999, Chief Operating Officer in 2001, and President and CEO in 2001.

Larry is a member and the immediate past chair of the Board of Visitors and Governors of his alma mater, Washington College, and also serves on the Wake Forest University Board of Trustees. Previously, Larry was a Senior Lecturer at Harvard Business School, where he focused on leadership, strategy and general management in the MBA and executive education programs.

A member of Phi Beta Kappa, Larry earned a B.A. in Economics from Washington College and an MBA from Harvard Business School.

This webpage is a biographical profile of H. Lawrence "Larry" Culp, Chairman and CEO of GE Aerospace (and former Chairman and CEO of GE). Key points include:

- Larry Culp is GE's twelfth CEO and eleventh Chairman. He joined the GE Board of Directors in April 2018, was appointed CEO of GE in October 2018, and was appointed CEO of GE Aerospace in June 2022.
- Under his leadership, GE's total gross debt reduction exceeded $90 billion through 2022. He championed lean practices, created nearly thirty P&Ls to increase operational visibility, and led GE's portfolio transformation including the sales of GE Capital Aviation Services (GECAS), Lighting, and BioPharma, as well as the spin of GE Transportation and its merger with Wabtec.
- In November 2021, GE announced plans to form three public companies focused on aviation, healthcare, and energy. Culp was slated to serve as non-executive chairman of the GE healthcare company upon its spin-off in early 2023, and planned to lead the aviation-focused company after the spin-off of GE Renewable Energy and Power businesses.
- Prior to GE, Culp served as President and CEO of Danaher Corporation from 2000 to 2014, during which the company increased revenues and market capitalization five-fold. He joined Danaher in 1990 and held various roles including President, Group Executive, COO, and CEO.
- He is a member and immediate past chair of the Board of Visitors and Governors of Washington College (his alma mater) and serves on the Wake Forest University Board of Trustees. He previously was a Senior Lecturer at Harvard Business School.
- Education: B.A. in Economics from Washington College and an MBA from Harvard Business School. He is a member of Phi Beta Kappa.

Let's head down to the Farnborough Airshow where Bloomberg's Guy Johnson is with the GE Aerospace chairman and CEO Larry Culp. Guy. I certainly am. Thank you very much indeed, Danny. Yes, welcome back to the Farnborough Airshow here in the UK. As you say, Larry Culp is with me. Larry, great to see you. Thanks for spending some time with us. Look, the first thing I've got to ask you is why on earth are we sitting in front of a very big 747 with your name on it? Well, it's the GE Aerospace name. Guy, good to be with you. This is our flying test bed. As you say, this is a 747-400. This is basically our airborne laboratory upon which we test all of our engines. There's a lot of talk here at Farnborough as there often is at the air shows around the future of flight. We wanted to bring the flying test bed up to Farnborough just to reinforce and help people understand everything that we do on board and inside the plane to make sure that we're bringing forward the best possible engines from a safety and reliability perspective. You going to test the next generation of of engines for for narrow-bodies like the 737s or the A320s on this cuz there's a big debate here at Farnborough about whether it's it's open rotor or the traditional kind of ducted jet engine for that gen next generation. Is this the aircraft you'd use to test that? Very much so. So, even though it's a wide-body engine, we can test virtually any engine that we might fly across our portfolio under development on the flying test bed. Cool. Let's talk a little bit about the show and what has happened here. I'm sure you've been absolutely snowed under meeting after meeting. What what I've what I've seen come out of the show is again huge numbers of orders for aircraft which means huge numbers of orders for engines. You've just landed a huge deal in India as well. The backlog is getting bigger and bigger, Larry. It's a nice problem to have, but at some point are you going to have to invest in additional manufacturing kit in order to fulfill some of these huge orders that you're taking? Well, guys, it's been very busy. We've been here since Saturday and I don't think we've had a better air show. From an orders perspective, we've had a number of announcements. I think the one you're referring to is one we let let out yesterday afternoon. Over 1,000 engines with Indigo Airlines in India. Really excited about that multi-year commitment. There are others. I won't take our limited time here to go through the roster of them. There are many. There are many. Narrow body and wide body. Guy, we've been investing in our manufacturing footprint and our supply chain for years. We know that a good air show is interesting, but we're on a multi-year ramp both with our commercial customers and in defense. Right, we're sold out into the early 2030s. So, whether it be investments in fixed capital, just as importantly investments in people and process, those are the things that enabled us say in the first half of this year to increase our engine deliveries by over 30% year-over-year. We're going to need need to be driving that sort of improvement that that sort of growth for years to come. Does that pace increase? Does does the cadence of that start to to increase? As you say, you're sold out for years and years to come. Well, I don't think we need to necessarily compound at 30%, but we're going to have to do more in the second half of this year Yep. than we did in the first half and '27 is going to need to be bigger than '26. So, we know we're on a multi-year ramp and what I'm so excited about, we said this last Thursday at our earnings call, we've got nine quarters in a row now where we've seen double-digit sequential increases from our suppliers that are probably prone to the us the most, which tells me they're investing or collaborating to break bottlenecks where they exist, and we're able to get more from them. In turn, we're able to deliver more to our airframe and airline customers. you think you're going to have to invest more in that? You You did highlight that. It was something that really stood out in terms of what you said on that earnings call. But But is there something Do you think you're going to have to invest more in that supply chain? I We've talked about kind of investing in in your capital infrastructure. Do you think you're going to have to invest in that? Is Is there M&A stories that you maybe you think about in order to just get that supply chain to where you want it to be? There is There is more to come with that without doubt. Most of that will be organic, right? Within our operations, some of it will come by way of collaboration. I'm sure there'll be inorganic investments as well. We've done a number of small acquisitions with suppliers that were better off, frankly, under our roof than at arm's length. But at the end of the day, it's not about ownership. It's about problem identification and breaking those constraints. Again, I think we made a lot of progress the last few years in partnership with a number of our key suppliers, large and small, many of them here. Uh more to come. Okay. There's been so much news flow as we've been here at the at the show. One of them has been around what is happening with oil prices and the fact that we're seeing them heading back up again as a result of what's happening in the Gulf right now. If I talk to Kelly over at Boeing, if I talk to Guillaume at Airbus, they're like, this is This is in some ways good news for us cuz all it does is it encourages our customers, the airlines, to invest in the most up-to-date aircraft, most fuel-efficient aircraft that they can get their hands on. For you though, I I just wonder whether it's a slightly different story because what we do see as well is that the airlines look at their older fleets and go, "Maybe we should retire some of those older aircraft." But the spare parts business is a big margin driver for you. How do you see the balance working there? Well, I would say what's good for Boeing or good for Airbus is good for General Electric. There's There's no two ways about that. But the other piece of the equation right now, Guy, that you didn't touch on, frankly, is demand. Every airline CEO that has been at at Farnborough, those that we talked to at just a few weeks ago at at IATA in Rio, Yep. all have remarked about how strong demand has been even in the face of some of the oil price disruptions since the springtime. So, we're looking at a situation where we have very strong aftermarket demand. We have very strong new make demand. And again, we can never forget about defense. So, we have our we have our work cut out for us on a multi-year basis. We know we're going to have to ramp, we're going to make those investments, drive those process improvements, but that work is underway at GE Aerospace, and that work will continue. One of the big discussions here has been almost about the aircraft that's not here, and that's the next generation of narrow body. We talked about it a little bit earlier on. You're going to test it on this 747, the engine for that. You're pushing quite hard for the open rotor technology. You think that's the future. You think it's going to be simpler, easier to maintain, have have some fairly big cost efficiencies that come with it. The airframers aren't there yet. They're not They don't appear ready, judging by the conversations that I've had, to be ready to make a decision on that. How late can they leave it? When do you think that decision is going to come? Well, we had an announcement just yesterday in concert with Airbus, Yep. with CFM International, and we were talking about our our new flying test bed equivalent for the the open fan architecture. It's a technology development program. Guy, as as you well know, this is a multi-year effort. We do think the open fan architecture provides both efficiency and maintenance or cost of ownership benefits. So, we think we will ultimately be able to deliver to the airlines, the ultimate customer, an opportunity to do to do both. It's not yet a product, so there's there's work to do here. There's plenty of time for us all to work that out, but every next generation narrow body has always come forward with a step function improvement in performance. Very hard to justify the investment to develop one but will not buy one without that. We're confident that the open fan architecture is going to be the enabler in that regard. Larry, it's always a pleasure. Thank you very much indeed for spending a little bit of time with us here at the Farnborough Airshow. We greatly appreciate it. Larry Culp, the CEO of GE Aerospace joining us here at Farnborough.

# Biography

![H. Lawrence Culp, Jr.](/system/files-encrypted/styles/large/encrypt/nasdaq_kms/people/2022/12/29/11-00-06/CS21002-01%20Larry_Culp-Crop-2704x3945_R1_resized.jpg?itok=zcDvia4k)

### H. Lawrence Culp, Jr.

Chairman

Mr. Culp is the Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of GE Aerospace. Mr. Culp joined the GE Board of Directors in April 2018 and was appointed Chief Executive Officer of GE in October 2018. In June 2022, he assumed additional duty as Chief Executive Officer of GE Aerospace and became Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of GE Aerospace when it launched as a public company in April 2024. He has also served as the non-executive Chairman of our Board since the Spin-Off. As Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of GE, Mr. Culp led the industrial technology Company’s multi-year financial and operational transformation. Under his leadership, GE further focused the company’s portfolio and simultaneously improved operations across its businesses by implementing and adopting lean with a relentless focus on safety, quality, delivery, and cost—in that order—to better serve customers. These efforts built a strong foundation for the successful creation of three independent, investment-grade public companies GE HealthCare, GE Vernova, and GE Aerospace. Each company is an industry leader with extensive global installed bases and a strong services orientation.

Prior to joining GE, Mr. Culp spent 25 years at Danaher Corporation, including serving as President and Chief Executive Officer from 2001 to 2014. Mr. Culp joined Danaher in 1990 at Veeder-Root, becoming President in 1993. He was appointed Group Executive and Corporate Officer in 1995, with responsibility for Danaher’s Environmental and Electronic Test and Measurement platforms while also serving as President of Fluke and Fluke Networks. He was named Executive Vice President in 1999, Chief Operating Officer in 2000, and President and Chief Executive Officer in 2001. Mr. Culp is a graduate of Washington College and Harvard Business School, and he served as a Senior Lecturer at Harvard Business School from 2015 to 2018. He is a member and former Chairman of the Board of Visitors & Governors of Washington College and also serves as a member of the Board of Trustees of Wake Forest University.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Patrick Pouyanné is a French businessman and engineer, born June 24, 1963, in Le Petit-Quevilly, Normandy, France. He has served as Chairman and CEO of TotalEnergies since 2014, one of the world's largest petroleum companies.

EDUCATION AND EARLY CAREER: Pouyanné entered the École Polytechnique at age 20 and graduated with an engineering degree, later also attending Mines ParisTech. He began his career in 1989 at the French Ministry of Industry. In 1993, he became technical advisor to French Prime Minister Édouard Balladur, and from 1995-1996 served as technical advisor for environment and industry and chief of staff to François Fillon at the Information Technology and Space Ministry.

CAREER AT TOTAL: In January 1997, Pouyanné joined the petroleum company Elf as general secretary for its Angolan subsidiary, later managing Qatar's exploration-production department. When Total absorbed Elf in 2000, he retained his position. He rose through the ranks: Senior VP of exploration production (finance, economics, information systems) in 2002; in charge of strategy, business development and R&D in 2006; joined Total's management committee in May 2006; deputy general manager of refining and chemistry in 2011; president of refining chemicals and member of the executive committee in 2012. Following the death of CEO Christophe de Margerie in October 2014, Pouyanné was appointed CEO and president of the executive committee (with Thierry Desmarest as temporary president). In May 2015 he was elected to the board, and in December 2015 he was appointed chairman and CEO, combining both roles.

OTHER ACTIVITIES: Pouyanné is a member of the Board of Directors of Capgemini (since 2017), a member of the Board of Trustees of the Brookings Institution, a member of the European Round Table of Industrialists (ERT), a member of the Board of Directors of the Polytechnic Institute of Paris (since 2019), and a member of The Business Council. He was decorated as Knight of the Legion of Honour in September 2015. He attended a dinner with U.S. President Donald Trump at the 2018 World Economic Forum in Davos and was a guest at the December 2022 White House state dinner hosted by President Joe Biden in honor of French President Emmanuel Macron.

EARLY LIFE & EDUCATION: Born in Västervik, Sweden, his family moved to Malmö when he was one, and later lived throughout Sweden, Germany, and Switzerland. At 16, his family moved to Stockholm. He completed military service at the Swedish Armed Forces Interpreter School (Tolkskolan) before university. He graduated from the Stockholm School of Economics with a master's degree (including an exchange semester at University of St. Gallen) and earned a CEMS Master in International Management and Finance and Accounting.

CAREER: He began his career in 1993 at Daimler-Benz AG, working on the finance team for setting up production of the Mercedes M-class at a new Alabama plant. In 2003, he became director of operations at McLaren; in 2005, he became managing director of Mercedes-Benz High Performance Engines (F1 engine factory). He moved back to the US in 2009 to head Mercedes-Benz's US division, returned to Germany in 2010 to chair Mercedes-AMG GmbH (relinquished to Tobias Moers on 1 October 2013). He joined the executive board of Mercedes-Benz Cars in October 2013 (marketing and sales), was appointed to the Daimler AG board of management on 1 January 2015, and took over Group Research and Mercedes-Benz Cars Development on 1 January 2017. He succeeded Dieter Zetsche as Chairman of the Board of Management in May 2019. In 2023, Mercedes-Benz extended his contract until mid-2029. As CEO, he accompanied Chancellor Olaf Scholz on a state visit to China in 2024.

POSITIONS: Källenius is a strong advocate of plug-in hybrids and electric vehicles. He pushed the EQ electric model initiative and a $12 billion investment into battery-powered vehicles, advocating for ten new purely electric models by 2022. The first was the Mercedes-Benz EQC SUV, launched in the first half of 2019.

PERSONAL LIFE: He is married to Sabine, an environmental activist with the Green Globe Organisation, who urged him to transition the entire Mercedes-Benz range (including the G-Wagon) to fully plug-in electric vehicles. They have three sons. He obtained German citizenship in July 2023. He is fluent in English, Swedish, and German. During his studies he was a member of the Danderyd Mean Machines American football team.

Key topics covered in the interview:

2. **Formula One relevance**: The Mercedes brand was "born on the racetrack." 3. **Evolution of luxury**: Källenius discusses how car aesthetics still matter and the need to reinvent modern luxury, blending digital and analog worlds—described as "a high-end Swiss watch with Apple functionality." 5. **Software transformation (MBOS)**: Mercedes-Benz has shifted from being a software integrator (where suppliers developed most software) to becoming "the architect" of the software stack and chipset. The new GLC is the first full-scale launch of MBOS (Mercedes-Benz Operating System), where every bit of the car is "reachable over the air," meaning cars "don't age digitally" and get better over time through downloadable functionality.

6. **Autonomous driving**: Mercedes began its first autonomous driving project in the 1980s. 7. **Innovation as commodity**: Källenius acknowledges that innovations like the airbag, ABS, ESP, and PRE-SAFE started at Mercedes and eventually became standard in all cars, which he views positively ("it makes traffic safer"). Mercedes' role is to lead at the top end of the market and move to the next innovation when previous ones become commoditized.

8. **Uhlenhaut Coupé**: The interview takes place in front of the 1950s Uhlenhaut Coupé racing car, whose spare was auctioned for €135 million (the most expensive car ever sold). Proceeds fund engineering and sustainability projects for young people worldwide.

The interview was conducted by Javier of the Morgan Stanley European auto team, who visited the Mercedes-Benz Museum for an early look at the new electric GLC.

Under Lei, Xiaomi became the world's third largest smartphone manufacturer in 2014 (behind Samsung and Apple), and Lei was widely known as the "Steve Jobs of China." In 2018, he oversaw Xiaomi's IPO on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, raising about $3 billion.

<summary>
This is the web version of Fortune's "The Modern Board" newsletter, written by Aman Kidwai and published July 15, 2022, focusing on corporate leadership and board governance trends.

MAIN STORY - The dual CEO-chairman role is losing favor on public boards: According to a new survey from The Conference Board using data from ESGAUGE (shared exclusively with Fortune), the percentage of S&P 500 companies combining the board chair and CEO roles dropped from 49% in 2018 to 44% in 2022, while companies with an independent board chair increased from 30% to 37% in the same period. <summary>

Written during the 2012 U.S. proxy season, the piece addresses the growing shareholder pressure for independent chairman roles and analyzes international variations in board leadership practices.

Key findings include:
- Board leadership structures depend on applicable laws/regulations and vary significantly across countries (Canada, Germany, UK, US), with no "one size fits all" solution to governance issues.
- Proponents of split CEO/chairman structures argue this model best positions companies for strong performance, while opponents note there is no irrefutable data proving split structures outperform combined ones and argue combination eliminates confusion and duplication.
- Spencer Stuart US Board Index data (2003–2011) shows a significant trend toward separation: companies combining CEO/chairman roles declined from 77% in 2003 to 59% in 2011, while those splitting roles rose from 23% to 41%. Independent non-executive chairmen increased from 9% (2004) to 21% (2011).

- Deloitte's analysis of S&P 500 proxy statements (Jan 1–March 20, 2012) found only 20 companies had a current chairman emeritus designation. The chairman emeritus is an honorary title often granted to former chairmen to acknowledge contributions, maintain institutional knowledge, and preserve relationships—with duties varying by company and the title being rescindable at any time.
- The article advises boards to evaluate optimal leadership structures considering company circumstances, regulatory environment, costs/benefits, and recommends defining evaluation criteria, responsibilities, and compensation for independent chair roles and chairman emeritus positions at the time these roles are created.
